AR-006 separately established that concurrent policy interventions (Operation Soteria, s 22C bail reform) may be mechanistically entangled with PolAir-Remote's own detection function, so their effects cannot simply be treated as independent and subtracted out. Section C of the Continuing Investigation Question Bank Answer Register (Q100-Q101) adds a third, geographically distinct confound that neither existing path names: youth offending/legal-action indicators also declined across the broader New England/North West police district and across Regional NSW as a whole over the same period.

This is not the same problem as AR-006's policy entanglement. A regional-scale trend would remain a live confound even in the hypothetical case where Soteria's and s 22C's specific contributions were fully isolated and subtracted, because it operates at the level of a wider geography rather than a named intervention. It means Moree's decline cannot be assumed distinctively Moree-specific - let alone specifically attributable to PolAir-Remote - without a comparator that separates what is common to the wider region from what, if anything, is particular to Moree.
determinations: Youth offending/legal-action indicators also declined across the broader New England/North West police district and Regional NSW as a whole over the same period as Moree's own decline.

This regional-scale trend is a distinct confound from the policy-mechanism entanglement already established in AR-006 - it would remain material even if Soteria's and s 22C bail reform's specific contributions were fully isolated.
No public matched-comparator analysis separates what is Moree-specific in the observed decline from what reflects the broader regional trend.
mechanisms: A causal claim narrowed to one town is harder to sustain once the same direction of change is documented at district and state-region scale, and disentangling the two requires a comparator design that does not currently exist publicly.
paths.boundary: No determination is made about the relative size of the region-wide component or whether Moree's decline exceeds the regional trend; only that the two have not been publicly separated.

paths.title: The Counterfactual Design Gap Now Has Named, Testable Components AR-006 Did Not Specify
analysis: AR-006 established, at a general level, that a credible counterfactual design (a matched comparator or interrupted time series) does not exist in the public record for Moree, and named falsifiers in principle (a post-deployment trend break surviving comparator controls; dose-response by drone exposure). Section C of the Answer Register (Q95-Q98, Q102-Q107) specifies particular components such a design would need that AR-006 did not itemise: whether offence-category changes are concentrated in categories most susceptible to aerial detection (Q102), whether a negative-control set of offences not materially affected by drone capability moved similarly over the same period (Q103), and whether the rate of decline itself changed distinguishably after January 2026 rather than merely continuing its pre-existing trajectory (Q97-Q98) - none of which the public record currently answers.

The same section also names two further candidate confounds beyond AR-006's Soteria/s 22C pairing that remain unapportioned - diversion or place-based programs, and ordinary policing changes (Q106-Q107) - and states three additional specific falsifiability tests beyond AR-006.3's two (Q108-Q109): disproportionate effect concentrated in drone-susceptible offences, equivalent movement in untreated comparator offences, and linked incident/cohort evidence showing outcomes materially attributable to drone tasking specifically. None of these tests has been publicly applied.
determinations: A negative-control offence-category test (offences not materially affected by drone capability, checked for parallel movement over the same period) is a specific, named component of the counterfactual design that the public record does not currently supply.
Diversion/place-based programs and ordinary policing changes join AR-006's Soteria/s 22C pairing as named components requiring apportionment that no public analysis currently performs.

Three additional specific falsifiability tests beyond AR-006.3's two - disproportionate effect in drone-susceptible offences, equivalent movement in untreated comparators, and linked incident/cohort evidence of drone-attributable outcomes - further specify how the causal hypothesis could be tested; none is currently applied in the public record.
mechanisms: Naming the specific tests a credible evaluation would require does not itself supply the offence-level data those tests depend on.
paths.boundary: No determination is made about what any of these tests would show if performed; only that the specific tests themselves, and the data they require, are now named and remain unperformed.

paths.title: Observation-to-Intervention Pipeline: Undisclosed Latency and Event Frequencies
analysis: AR-007 already established that the petition's "30-60 second deployment" claim measures aircraft launch/availability only, not the total time to a physical police response, and that the exact clock definition and its distributional statistics are undisclosed. Section D of the Continuing Investigation Question Bank Answer Register (Q111-Q115) extends this beyond the launch clock to the entire downstream chain: none of average arrival-over-incident time, average time until useful intelligence is relayed to ground police, average ground-police arrival time, average time from detection to physical intervention, or average time from detection to arrest is publicly disclosed, and none of them can be computed from the public record without linked mission/event timestamps and ground-unit records that do not exist publicly.

The same section (Q116-Q119) also asks how often specific pipeline outcomes occur rather than how long they take - how often the drone arrives before ground police, how often it locates a suspect before ground police arrive, how often ground officers are unavailable to act immediately on drone intelligence, and how many deployments produce useful intelligence but no immediate intervention. None of these frequencies is publicly disclosed either. Read together, the timing gap and the frequency gap describe the same undocumented chain from two angles - how long it takes, and how often it actually connects observation to action - neither of which AR-007's narrower launch-clock finding covers.
determinations: No average or distributional time figure - arrival over the incident, time to useful intelligence reaching ground police, ground-police arrival time, time to physical intervention, or time to arrest - is publicly disclosed for the observation-to-intervention pipeline.
Computing any of these times would require linked mission/event timestamps and ground-unit records that are not publicly available.

The frequency with which the drone arrives before ground police, locates a suspect before ground police arrive, encounters unavailable ground officers, or produces useful intelligence without an immediate intervention is likewise undisclosed.
mechanisms: Absence of published pipeline timing and frequency data is consistent with either the data not being collected in a linkable form, or being collected internally and not published; the public record does not distinguish these.
paths.boundary: No determination is made about the actual value of any of these times or frequencies, or about whether the underlying records exist internally but are simply unpublished versus not collected at all - only that none is publicly disclosed and none is computable from the public record checked. This extends AR-007's launch-clock finding to the downstream pipeline; it does not restate AR-007's own determinations about the 30-60 second claim itself.

paths.title: Structural Risk of a Growing Observation/Intervention Capacity Imbalance
analysis: Section D (Q125-Q127) of the Answer Register identifies a structural risk this investigation's other paths have not yet named: because a remote-observation platform can in principle scale detection capacity faster than physical-response capacity scales - additional aircraft, sensors and operators can extend how much is seen well ahead of any corresponding increase in frontline officers available to act on what is seen - the number of incidents detected could increase without physical-response capacity increasing to match. No public record establishes whether this occurred at Moree, whether local frontline staffing has been increased alongside the remote aerial observation capability, or whether any formal threshold or control exists that would prevent the imbalance from growing regardless.

Q120's separate question - whether PolAir-Remote has reduced dangerous vehicle pursuits - sits in the same gap from the outcome side. It is the one operational outcome named in this section not already covered by this investigation's existing undisclosed-outcome-measures findings (AR-029's response time, search time and ground-police workload; AR-030's equity-facing measures), and like those, no aggregate Moree result establishes whether it occurred. Absent that outcome data and absent staffing data, whether observation-capacity growth is translating into matched physical-intervention capability, or instead into a widening gap, is not answered either way by the public record.
determinations: A remote-observation platform can in principle scale detection capacity faster than physical-response capacity scales, creating a possible growing imbalance between what is detected and what can be acted on; whether this occurred at Moree is not established either way in the public record.
No public evidence shows local frontline staffing was increased alongside the remote aerial observation capability.
No public PolAir-specific threshold, control or fallback-capacity mechanism has been located that would prevent a growing observation/intervention imbalance if one exists.

Whether PolAir-Remote reduced dangerous vehicle pursuits - the one operational outcome in this section not already covered by AR-029/AR-030's undisclosed-outcome-measures findings - is likewise not established by any published aggregate Moree result.
mechanisms: Absence of published staffing, threshold and pursuit-outcome data is consistent with either the imbalance risk not materialising, or materialising without public disclosure; the public record does not distinguish these.
paths.boundary: No determination is made that a capacity imbalance has actually occurred, that staffing has not in fact increased through some unpublished channel, or that PolAir-Remote has or has not affected vehicle pursuits - only that the public record does not establish any of these, and that the mechanism by which an imbalance could occur is structurally plausible and currently unaddressed by any public control.

paths.title: Flight-Level Mission Data Schema and Disclosure Gap
analysis: Section E (Q128-Q149) of the Answer Register establishes that CASA's general operational-record baseline (referenced already by AR-019 for chain-of-custody purposes) does not resolve a distinct question: whether NSW Police's own mission-level dataset for PolAir-Remote assigns each flight a unique identifier, links it to an incident or event number, classifies it into a defined set of categories (reactive, proactive, training, testing, scheduled patrol, high-visibility operation, covert), and records what proportion of flights fall into each category. None of this classification structure, nor the geographic distribution data it would enable - areas of highest flight frequency, specific streets or neighbourhoods receiving repeated observation, areas of longest cumulative loiter time - is publicly disclosed.

A further, more granular layer is also undisclosed: whether flight-path geometry and altitude are retained beyond what the platform and CASA make technically possible, and whether sensor mode, zoom use, thermal use, recording status, operator identity, mid-flight purpose changes, and cross-flight tracking of the same person or vehicle across multiple separate missions are recorded and retained as distinct fields. This is a mission-data-schema gap, not a chain-of-custody gap: it concerns what NSW Police's own tasking and surveillance-footprint records contain, independent of whether any specific flight's imagery is later used as evidence.
determinations: NSW Police's own mission-level dataset structure - unique flight identifiers, incident linkage, and a defined flight-type classification with per-category proportions - is not publicly disclosed, beyond the general CASA record-keeping baseline AR-019 already established.
Geographic distribution data (areas of highest flight frequency, specific streets or neighbourhoods with repeated observation, areas of longest cumulative loiter time) is not publicly disclosed.

Granular per-flight technical fields (sensor mode, zoom, thermal use, recording status, operator identity, mid-flight purpose change, and cross-flight tracking of the same person or vehicle) are not confirmed as recorded or retained in the public record; flight-path and altitude retention are only partially established as technically possible, not confirmed as NSW Police's actual retention practice.
mechanisms: A general capability to log flights (CASA/platform) is publicly established; the specific schema NSW Police actually uses to classify and geographically aggregate PolAir-Remote flights is not.
paths.boundary: No determination is made about what NSW Police's actual internal mission-data schema contains; only that its structure and content are not publicly disclosed at the level of detail this section's questions specify.

paths.title: Flight-Geography Demographic and Spatial Disproportionality Analysis Gap
analysis: Section E (Q150-Q158) of the Answer Register establishes that joining flight geography against Aboriginal population distribution, offence location, socioeconomic disadvantage, and proactive-policing operations is technically feasible in principle - if a de-identified flight-geography dataset were released, it could be joined to already-public demographic, offence and spatial datasets - but NSW Police has not published that flight-geography dataset, so no such join has been performed by anyone outside the organisation.

Absent that dataset, none of this section's specific analytical questions - whether some communities are exposed to more aerial observation than their offence incidence would predict, whether private residential areas are disproportionately represented in flight paths, whether repeated patrol routes or predictable patrol times exist, and whether geographic or temporal displacement of activity has been assessed - can currently be answered from the public record. This is distinct from AR-015's consultation-sequencing finding (which concerns whether communities had input before deployment) and AR-012's biometric/AI-governance gap (which concerns identification technology): this path concerns whether the surveillance footprint itself, independent of any identification capability or consultation process, is disclosed and analysable for disproportionate spatial impact.
determinations: Joining flight geography against demographic and spatial datasets (Aboriginal population distribution, offence location, socioeconomic disadvantage, proactive-policing operations) is technically feasible in principle but has not been performed, because NSW Police has not published the underlying de-identified flight-geography dataset.

Whether any community is exposed to aerial observation disproportionate to its offence incidence, and whether private residential areas are disproportionately represented in flight paths, cannot currently be determined from the public record.

Whether flight patrol routes and times are repeated or predictable, and whether geographic or temporal displacement of activity has occurred, are open analytical questions requiring data not currently public.
mechanisms: The absence of a released flight-geography dataset prevents any independent disproportionality analysis; this does not establish that disproportionate exposure exists, only that it cannot currently be tested.
paths.boundary: No determination is made that flight patterns are or are not geographically or demographically disproportionate; only that the public record does not currently contain what would be needed to test this either way.

paths.title: Secondary-Detection Purpose-Change Authorization and Audit-Trail Gap
analysis: Section F (Q159-Q165, Q177) of the Answer Register addresses what happens the moment a PolAir-Remote mission tasked for one incident observes an unrelated possible offence. General policing law permits a new police event to be generated from lawfully obtained information, and legal-authority requirements for further action are fact-dependent rather than fixed - so neither of those general propositions is in dispute. What is not established is the PolAir-Remote-specific decision process itself: who authorises a mid-mission change of observation purpose, whether the operator must document the secondary purpose, whether a separate tasking record is created, and whether the same rule applies to live observation as to footage retained afterward.

This is a distinct governance layer from AR-010's reactive/proactive operating-mode contradiction, which concerns which overall mode the program uses, and from AR-019's evidence-handling/chain-of-custody gap, which concerns imagery once it is already being treated as courtroom evidence: this path concerns the internal decision moment at which a single mission's own scope expands, before any evidentiary or courtroom question arises. Q177's mandatory-audit-trail question is the most consequential of the eight items here, because its absence would mean the moment a mission's purpose changes is not necessarily independently reconstructable from any record at all.
determinations: No public PolAir-Remote-specific rule establishes who authorises a mid-mission change of observation purpose, or on what basis.
No public rule confirms mandatory documentation of a secondary purpose, a separate tasking record, or a distinct audit-trail requirement for purpose changes.
Whether the same authorization/documentation rule applies to live observation as to footage retained afterward is not established.

This gap concerns the internal decision process at the moment of purpose change, distinct from AR-019's evidentiary chain-of-custody gap (imagery already treated as courtroom evidence) and AR-010's operating-mode contradiction (the program's overall stated mode).
mechanisms: The absence of a public authorization/audit-trail rule for purpose changes is consistent with an internal rule existing but not being published, or with no such rule existing at all; the public record does not distinguish these.
paths.boundary: No determination is made that any purpose change has occurred without authorization or documentation in practice; only that no public rule establishes what that authorization or documentation requirement is.

paths.title: Downstream Legal-Escalation and Secondary-Detection Reporting Gap
analysis: The remaining thirteen items in Section F (Q166-Q176, Q178-Q179) concern what an incidental or secondary detection can lead to once it occurs. No public PolAir-Remote-specific rule or threshold establishes whether such a detection alone can justify a search, a pursuit, an arrest, or the creation of an intelligence record; whether incidental imagery can be retained after the originating mission ends, searched retrospectively for an unrelated investigation, or reused for another purpose without a fresh approval; or whether an unrelated person or vehicle observed only incidentally can be tracked, or thermal imaging and AI-assisted tracking activated once the mission's purpose has changed.

AR-020 already established that NSW law provides real, if circumstance-dependent, secondary-use pathways for law-enforcement information generally (PPIP Act s 23); this path is narrower and more operational - it asks whether PolAir-Remote specifically has a published threshold or process governing when an incidental detection converts into one of these further actions, and finds none. The final two items (Q178-Q179) compound the gap: secondary detections are not confirmed as tracked as a distinct operational category at all, so even the frequency with which incidental observation leads to further police action is unknown from the public record - there is no visible starting point from which to measure how often this pathway is actually used.
determinations: No public PolAir-Remote-specific threshold or process establishes whether an incidental/secondary detection alone can justify a search, pursuit, arrest, or intelligence record.

No public rule establishes whether incidental imagery can be retained past the originating mission, searched retrospectively for an unrelated investigation, or reused for another purpose without fresh approval.

No public rule establishes whether an unrelated person or vehicle observed incidentally can be tracked, or whether thermal imaging or AI-assisted tracking can be activated once a mission's purpose has changed.

Secondary detections are not confirmed as recorded or reported as a distinct operational category, so the frequency with which incidental observation leads to further police action is not established from the public record.
mechanisms: PPIP Act s 23 establishes that a legal pathway for this kind of secondary use exists in principle (AR-020); whether PolAir-Remote's own practice actually applies a defined threshold or process for it, or how often, is not publicly reconstructable.
paths.boundary: No determination is made that any incidental detection has in fact been used to justify a search, arrest, or tracking action, or that any of these have occurred without proper authority; only that no public threshold, process, or frequency data exists to test this.

paths.title: Private-Property Aerial Observation Boundary Is Not Publicly Defined
analysis: Section G (Q180-Q189) of the Answer Register puts ten specific, distinct questions to the public record about where the boundary of PolAir-Remote's permitted aerial observation of private property sits: yards, home exteriors, windows, deliberate viewing through windows, zoom into residential property, thermal observation of homes, prolonged loitering over residences, altitude or angle restrictions, and whether any of the foregoing differs between emergency response and proactive patrol, or when a person is suspected of an offence. Every one of the ten receives materially the same answer: no NSW Police PolAir-Remote-specific operational rule addressing that dimension has been publicly located, and general law is not shown to substitute for the missing police-specific limit.

This is a distinct governance layer from AR-012's AI/biometric-processing gap, which concerns what may be done with imagery once captured, and from AR-010's reactive/proactive operating-mode contradiction, which concerns which overall mode the program is described as using: this path concerns the prior question of where and how imagery of private property may be captured in the first place. Q188 asks directly whether the undisclosed boundary itself varies by operating mode, and Q189 whether it varies when a person is suspected of an offence - meaning even the conditions under which the boundary might shift are themselves undocumented, not only the boundary's substantive content.
determinations: No public PolAir-Remote-specific rule addresses any of ten distinct private-property observation-boundary dimensions tested: yards, home exteriors, windows, deliberate window viewing, zoom, thermal observation, loitering, altitude/angle, an emergency-versus-proactive-patrol distinction, or a suspected-offence distinction.
General law is not shown to substitute for the missing PolAir-Remote-specific limit on any of these ten dimensions.

Whether an undisclosed boundary, if one exists internally, varies between emergency response and proactive patrol, or when a person is suspected of an offence, is itself not established from the public record.
mechanisms: The materially identical answer recorded against all ten items is consistent with a single templated non-answer rather than ten independently-resolved negatives; the public record does not distinguish an unpublished internal rule from the absence of any rule at all.
paths.boundary: No determination is made about NSW Police's actual internal practice on any of these ten dimensions, or that any specific flight has observed private property in a manner that would breach an undocumented boundary; only that no public rule establishes where that boundary sits.

paths.title: Warrant-Authority Ambiguity and Absent Privacy-Incident/Complaint Architecture
analysis: The remaining nine items in Section G (Q190-Q198) shift from where the observation boundary sits (AR-042) to what governs crossing it and what happens afterward. Three items (Q190-Q192) establish that the applicable legal-authority and warrant-requirement questions are fact-specific rather than settled by any single public rule: the Surveillance Devices Act does not establish a blanket rule that every drone view of private property needs a warrant, and what other warrant or authority might be required depends on the operation type and the applicable police power, neither of which is specified in the abstract. The remaining six items (Q193-Q198) establish that no public PolAir-Remote-specific document names who advises operators approaching this boundary or what process exists if it is breached, accidentally or deliberately - and that whether privacy incidents are even logged as a distinct category, and how many complaints have been made or substantiated, are not established from the public record.

AR-016 already established that NSW's formal complaint architecture (principally the LECC) has clear, systemic jurisdiction over PolAir-Remote governance concerns, and that the practical accountability gap is a resident's inability to discover whether a specific flight occurred, not the absence of a complaint mechanism itself. Section G sharpens that finding one layer further: even setting the discoverability problem aside, no public record establishes that an internal escalation route or incident-logging process exists at all for the specific case of a suspected private-property observation-boundary breach, or that complaint volume or substantiation data for this category is tracked anywhere. A resident who does learn a flight occurred would still have no visible internal process shown to receive that concern, nor any published figure showing the mechanism has ever been used for this purpose.
determinations: No single public rule establishes a blanket legal authority or blanket warrant requirement for drone observation of private activity; both are stated to be fact-specific, and no public criteria establish how that fact-specific determination is to be made.
No public PolAir-Remote-specific document identifies an operational or legal adviser, or an escalation route, for private-property observation-boundary questions.
No public PolAir-Remote-specific process establishes what occurs following an accidental or deliberate observation-boundary breach.

Whether privacy incidents are logged as a distinct operational category, and the number of privacy complaints made or substantiated, are not established from the public record - extending AR-016's discoverability finding to the internal incident-tracking layer itself.
mechanisms: AR-016 established that a resident cannot discover whether a specific flight occurred; this section shows the internal incident-logging and complaint-count layer is not established as existing either, which would remain a barrier even if individual-flight discoverability were resolved.
paths.boundary: No determination is made that any observation-boundary breach has occurred, that any complaint has been filed, or that any complaint-handling failure has taken place; only that no public rule establishes the applicable warrant/authority test in specific terms, or confirms the existence of an incident-logging and complaint-count architecture for this category.

paths.title: Recording Discretion and Captured-Data Scope Undisclosed
analysis: NSW Police's own public launch messaging establishes that PolAir-Remote flights are not recorded by default and that live video can be streamed without being recorded, meaning a routine flight can occur with no retained visual record at all. This confirms recording is discretionary rather than universal, but does not establish what triggers the discretion: who decides that a given flight moves from unrecorded live viewing into recorded evidentiary capture, and on what criteria, is not publicly disclosed.

The undisclosed scope extends beyond the recording/non-recording decision itself. Whether audio is collected on any Moree flight, whether still images are automatically generated, and what evidentiary metadata (beyond the general technical capability drone systems have to attach timestamps and location) NSW Police actually preserves are all unestablished from the public record. Together these mean the true evidentiary footprint of any given flight - what was captured, in what form, and why - cannot currently be reconstructed from outside the organisation.
determinations: NSW Police's own messaging establishes that recording is not default or universal for PolAir-Remote flights, and that unrecorded live viewing is a normal, stated operating mode rather than an edge case.
The decision authority and the triggering criteria for moving a flight from unrecorded viewing into recorded capture are not publicly disclosed.

Whether audio is collected and whether still images are automatically generated are both undisclosed for the Moree implementation specifically, despite general platform technical capability to do either.
The exact metadata NSW Police preserves with captured imagery is not publicly specified beyond generic platform technical capability.
mechanisms: A confirmed non-default recording practice paired with an undisclosed capture trigger and undisclosed capture scope means the actual evidentiary footprint of a given flight cannot be determined from the public record alone.
paths.boundary: No determination is made that any specific flight was, or was not, appropriately recorded, or that audio, stills or particular metadata were, or were not, captured on any occasion; only that the criteria governing when capture occurs and its full technical scope are not publicly disclosed.

paths.title: Retention, Access and Secondary-Use Governance Gap for PolAir-Remote Data
analysis: Beyond CASA's seven-year requirement for specified aviation records already established by AR-019, no PolAir-Remote-specific retention period is publicly disclosed for any of the four data classes checked - evidentiary footage, non-evidentiary footage, incidental imagery, or telemetry. Even for flight logs, where a CASA minimum is known, whether NSW Police retains material for longer or handles it differently from that minimum is not established. Nor is it established whether these retention periods operate automatically or at discretion, who may extend them, or what reason - if any - must be documented for doing so.

A second, distinct governance layer concerns what happens to material once retained: no public rule establishes who may access it, or whether authorised or unauthorised access is logged; whether it can be copied to another NSW Police system or provided to another agency; or whether it can be used for intelligence analysis, for training, to develop AI models, or later analysed for a purpose not contemplated when it was collected. Deletion itself is equally undocumented - no public verification mechanism for deletion is established, and no public record addresses what happens to retained data if the program is terminated. Read together, these items describe a single undocumented control layer spanning the entire lifecycle of PolAir-Remote-derived data after capture - how long it is kept, who may use it for what, and how its eventual disposal is verified - none of which is publicly disclosed.
determinations: No PolAir-Remote-specific retention period is publicly disclosed for evidentiary footage, non-evidentiary footage, incidental imagery, or telemetry; even for flight logs, where a CASA minimum exists, whether NSW Police retains material longer or handles it differently is undisclosed.
Whether retention periods operate automatically or at discretion, who may extend them, and what reason must be documented for an extension are all undisclosed.
No public rule establishes who may access retained PolAir-Remote material, or whether authorised or unauthorised access attempts are logged.

No public rule establishes whether retained material can be copied to another NSW Police system, provided to another agency, used for intelligence analysis or training, used to develop AI models, or later analysed for a purpose not contemplated when it was collected.
No public deletion-verification mechanism is established, and no public record addresses the disposition of retained data if the program is terminated.
mechanisms: The complete data-lifecycle governance framework covering retention, access and secondary use of PolAir-Remote-derived material is not publicly reconstructable from any source located.
paths.boundary: No determination is made that PolAir-Remote data has ever been retained, accessed, shared, or used for a secondary purpose improperly, or that any deletion has failed to occur; only that the governing retention, access, and secondary-use rules are not publicly disclosed, so none of this can currently be independently tested.

paths.title: Onboard and Centralized AI Function Enablement Undisclosed
analysis: The Matrice 4-series platform Moree PolAir-Remote uses is documented (AR-012, AR-019) as technically capable of AI-assisted person and object detection and tracking, but whether any specific function is actually enabled in the Moree deployment is a separate, undisclosed question this investigation had not yet tested item by item. No public record confirms or denies whether human-subject detection, vehicle detection, automatic subject tracking, or automatic reacquisition is switched on for Moree aircraft, whether custom AI models beyond the vendor default have been installed, or whether any third-party analytics platform is connected to the operational workflow.

The same undisclosed-enablement gap extends to automation and centralized processing beyond the aircraft itself: whether alarm-triggered automated launches or scheduled autonomous patrols are enabled, and whether the Remote Operations Centre performs any centralized automated video, object, or person detection on the imagery it receives, are all unestablished from the public record checked. Together, these items describe the full range of automated and semi-automated capability the platform could exercise in practice - from what a single aircraft's onboard system does with what it sees, to what a human-monitored central operations centre does with the aggregate feed - and none of it is confirmed as either present or absent.
determinations: Whether onboard human-subject detection, vehicle detection, automatic subject tracking, or automatic reacquisition is enabled on Moree aircraft is not publicly disclosed, despite the underlying platform's technical capability to run each function being established.
Whether custom AI models beyond the vendor default are installed, or third-party analytics are connected to the operational workflow, is not publicly disclosed.
Whether alarm-triggered automated launches or scheduled autonomous patrols are enabled is not publicly disclosed.
Whether the Remote Operations Centre performs any centralized automated video, object, or person detection on received imagery is not publicly disclosed.
mechanisms: A documented technical capability paired with an undisclosed operational enablement status means the platform's actual automated behaviour in Moree cannot be determined from the public record alone.
paths.boundary: No determination is made that any of these AI or automation functions is, or is not, currently enabled or in use on Moree PolAir-Remote aircraft or at the Remote Operations Centre; only that their enablement status is not publicly disclosed either way.

paths.title: Biometric Authorization Pathway and AI Risk-Governance Process Undisclosed
analysis: AR-012 already established that no public NSW AI Assessment Framework determination for PolAir-Remote has been located, and that no current facial-recognition or biometric-matching use is established even though state-level system-linkage capability exists. This section's remaining items go beyond that headline finding to the specific mechanics and process controls that would govern biometric use if it occurred: whether an individual frame can be manually submitted for face-matching, and whether recorded imagery can specifically be submitted to the National Facial Biometric Matching Capability, are both undisclosed as operational pathways distinct from the general state-level infrastructure AR-012 already names. So is the authority that would permit such a use, and whether biometric use is affirmatively prohibited absent separate approval; no PolAir-specific Privacy Impact Assessment considering biometric linkage has been publicly located.

A second, adjacent process gap concerns AI risk governance generally, independent of biometrics specifically: no public record discloses what risk level, if any, has been assigned to PolAir-Remote's AI functions, who approved their use, whether AI false positives are measured, or whether an AI detection is required to be verified by a human before it can generate police action - or, indeed, whether an automated detection can generate police action on its own at all. Nor is it established what reassessment process, if any, is triggered when software features change or a new AI model is added, or whether any public capability register exists listing which AI functions are currently enabled or disabled. Read together with AR-046's separate finding that the underlying enablement status of these same functions is itself undisclosed, this means neither what the system does nor the governance process that would control what it does is publicly documented.
determinations: No operational pathway is disclosed for manually submitting an individual frame, or specifically submitting recorded PolAir-Remote imagery, to the National Facial Biometric Matching Capability - a narrower gap than AR-012's general finding that state-level biometric-matching infrastructure exists.

The authority that would permit a biometric submission, and whether biometric use is affirmatively prohibited absent separate approval, are both undisclosed; no PolAir-specific Privacy Impact Assessment considering biometric linkage has been publicly located.

No public risk level, approval record, false-positive measurement, or human-verification requirement is disclosed for PolAir-Remote's AI functions, nor is it established whether an automated AI detection can generate police action without human verification.
No public reassessment process is disclosed for when software features change or a new AI model is added, and no public capability register lists which AI functions are enabled or disabled.
mechanisms: The specific authorization pathway, risk-governance record, and capability register that would let an outside party test whether PolAir-Remote's AI and biometric capability is being used within any stated limit are not publicly reconstructable from any source located.
paths.boundary: No determination is made that any biometric submission has occurred, that any AI detection has generated police action without verification, or that any risk assessment does not exist internally; only that none of this is publicly disclosed, so it cannot currently be independently tested.

paths.title: Data Storage Location, Cross-Border Transfer and Vendor/Support Access Undisclosed
analysis: Where PolAir-Remote's live video, recorded video, flight logs and telemetry are actually processed and stored is not publicly disclosed for any of the four data classes, despite the platform's manufacturer offering both cloud-connected (DJI cloud infrastructure, FlightHub 2) and privacy-protective local-only (Local Data Mode, disabled manufacturer-cloud-connection) configuration options. Whether NSW Police uses the cloud-connected option, the local-only option, or some other arrangement for the Moree deployment - and, if FlightHub 2 is used, whether it is hosted by the vendor or run on-premises - is not established from any source located.

This configuration choice has a direct cross-border and third-party-access dimension: whether any operational data or telemetry leaves Australia, whether DJI personnel can access any of it, whether another vendor can access it, and where the personnel providing technical support are located are all unresolved from the public record. None of these questions can be answered by inference from the platform's general technical capability alone, since the same hardware supports materially different configurations with materially different jurisdictional exposure.
determinations: The operational storage/processing location is undisclosed for all four data classes checked - live video, recorded video, flight logs, and telemetry.

Whether DJI's cloud-connected features (DJI cloud infrastructure, FlightHub 2, and if so hosted versus on-premises) or its privacy-protective local-only options (Local Data Mode, disabled manufacturer cloud connections) are the ones actually configured for the Moree deployment is undisclosed.
Whether any operational data or telemetry leaves Australia, and whether DJI personnel or another vendor can access it, are both unresolved from the public record.
The location of the personnel providing technical support for the system - a proxy for the jurisdictional exposure of any remote-access channel - is undisclosed.
mechanisms: A platform capable of materially different data-sovereignty configurations, paired with no disclosure of which configuration is actually in use, means jurisdictional exposure cannot be assessed from the public record alone.
paths.boundary: No determination is made that any PolAir-Remote data has actually left Australia, or that DJI or another vendor has actually accessed it, or that any privacy-protective configuration option is disabled; only that which configuration is in use, and therefore what cross-border or third-party access is possible, is not publicly disclosed.

paths.title: Cybersecurity Assurance and Update-Governance Gap
analysis: Beyond AR-013's existing finding that no NSW-Police-specific DJI supply-chain risk assessment has been located, this section establishes that the same gap extends to every other formal security-assurance step checked: no penetration test, no general cyber-security risk assessment, and no foreign-ownership/control/influence (FOCI) assessment specific to the Moree configuration has been publicly located either - and because no assessment of any kind has been located, no specific risk finding for DJI and no required mitigation has been publicly disclosed. No public document discloses the rationale by which the Moree configuration was itself assessed as acceptable for NSW Police use, a decision-record gap distinct from, and beyond, the absence of the assessments that would ordinarily feed into it.

A second, related gap concerns the technical controls actually protecting the system day to day, and the process governing how the system changes over time. The vendor platform supports encrypted communications and storage and enterprise-grade authentication, but the specific NSW Police configuration - live-transmission and stored-data encryption, operator authentication, whether multi-factor authentication is mandatory, privileged-access controls, and whether system logs are centrally monitored - is undisclosed. Change management is undisclosed in the same way: vendor remote support is technically possible on platforms of this kind, and firmware/software updates are established as capable of changing security posture and operational capability, but whether remote support is enabled or contracted for NSW Police, who approves a firmware or software update, and whether each update is security-assessed before deployment are all unresolved.
determinations: Beyond AR-013.4's existing finding that no DJI supply-chain risk assessment has been located, no penetration test, general cyber-security risk assessment, or foreign-ownership/control/influence assessment specific to the Moree configuration has been publicly located either, and no risk finding or required mitigation for DJI has been publicly disclosed as a result.
No public document discloses the rationale by which the Moree DJI-manufactured configuration was assessed as acceptable for NSW Police use.

The specific technical controls protecting live transmission and stored data (encryption configuration) and controlling system access (authentication, mandatory multi-factor authentication, privileged-access controls, centralized log monitoring) are undisclosed beyond generic vendor-platform capability.

Whether vendor remote support is enabled or contracted for NSW Police, who approves a firmware or software update, and whether each update is security-assessed before deployment are all undisclosed, despite firmware/software updates being established as capable of changing security posture and operational capability.
mechanisms: The complete security-assurance and change-management framework governing PolAir-Remote - what was assessed, what was found, what controls are configured, and who approves a change - is not publicly reconstructable from any source located.
paths.boundary: No determination is made that any specific technical control is absent or inadequate, that a vulnerability exists, that vendor remote access has occurred, or that the Moree configuration's acceptance was unjustified; only that the assurance processes, their outcomes, and the ongoing change-management controls are not publicly disclosed, so none of this can currently be independently tested.

paths.title: RPAS Panel and Contract Architecture: Twenty Undisclosed Terms Beyond AR-013's General Outcome Gap
analysis: AR-013 already established that neither EOI's outcome (supplier, contract value, scope) is currently publicly disclosed. This section tests that gap at the level of specific, named contract terms rather than restating it in general: whether the RPAS panel itself has been formally established, which suppliers (if any) were selected or shortlisted, and whether any contract has been executed are all undisclosed at the threshold level - before any question of contract content arises.

Beyond that threshold question, none of eighteen specific contract-term dimensions checked is publicly disclosed for any contract that may exist: value, duration, the goods/services and geographic scope covered, whether Remote Operations Centre services, autonomous dock systems, specialist payloads, AI functionality, software subscriptions, or data hosting are included, whether support from overseas personnel is included, whether the contract permits future capability additions without a new procurement process, exit rights, data-return and deletion obligations, cyber-security requirements, Australian data-location requirements, restrictions on foreign cloud services, and a requirement to notify ownership/control changes. None of these eighteen dimensions is addressed even in outline by AR-013's own text, which speaks only to the fact that an outcome is undisclosed, not to what the contract terms would need to cover once one is.
determinations: Whether the RPAS panel contemplated by EOI YR-2026-0058 has been formally established, and whether any supplier has been selected, shortlisted, or contracted, is undisclosed.

None of eighteen specific contract-term dimensions - value, duration, scope of goods/services, geographic scope, Remote Operations Centre services, autonomous dock systems, specialist payloads, AI functionality, software subscriptions, data hosting, overseas-personnel support, future-capability-addition rights, exit rights, data-return/deletion obligations, cyber-security requirements, Australian data-location requirements, foreign-cloud-service restrictions, and ownership/control-change notification - is publicly disclosed for any RPAS-related contract that may exist.
This is a more granular, named-component extension of AR-013.3's general "outcome not disclosed" finding, in the same manner AR-033 extended AR-005 and AR-048 extended AR-019/AR-020.
mechanisms: Neither the existence of a panel or supplier relationship, nor any of eighteen specific contract terms that would govern its scope, cost, data handling, and exit conditions, is publicly reconstructable from any source located.
paths.boundary: No determination is made that a panel has not been established, that no supplier has been selected, or that any specific contract term is absent, inadequate, or improperly negotiated; only that none of this is publicly disclosed, so it cannot currently be independently verified either way.

paths.title: Aviation Command Operating Model Review: Whether Alternatives to RPAS Expansion Were Ever Evaluated Is Undisclosed
analysis: AR-013.2 already established that PolAir-Remote/RPAS decisions sit inside a broader Aviation Command operating-model review rather than a standalone procurement. This section extends that finding to the review's substance and outcome: the review's own findings and recommendations have not been publicly located, so whether any recommendation has been adopted, and whether any subsequent procurement has flowed from it, cannot be established from the public record.

More specifically, no completed review is public showing whether the review evaluated an option of not expanding remotely piloted aircraft at all, or an alternative of investing in additional frontline staffing instead of aircraft. The EOI's own published scope covers governance, regulatory compliance, workforce, training, fleet, and operational efficiency broadly, which is consistent with either alternative being considered or neither being considered - the scope document alone does not resolve it.
determinations: The Aviation Command Operating Model Review's own findings and recommendations have not been publicly located, so whether any recommendation was adopted or has led to subsequent procurement is undisclosed.

Whether the review evaluated an option of not expanding remotely piloted aircraft, or an alternative of investing in additional frontline staffing, is undisclosed; the EOI's published scope does not resolve either question.
mechanisms: A command-wide review whose scope predates and encloses the RPAS expansion decision has produced no publicly located findings, so whether it considered any alternative to expansion cannot currently be tested.
paths.boundary: No determination is made that the review failed to consider an alternative, or that RPAS expansion was decided without genuine consideration of options; only that whether it did so is not publicly disclosed.

paths.title: Sunk-Cost Commitment Inventory Preceding the Moree Trial Evaluation
analysis: AR-014 already establishes that PolAir-Remote continued operating past its own stated six-month window with no located public exit criteria. Section L of the separate answer-register-l-to-t-run001.txt file (Q313-Q322) adds the concrete substrate underlying that finding: a real, multi-category commitment base already existed before any trial evaluation was completed, even though its financial scale is not public. Operational dock and aircraft infrastructure was installed in Moree, a linked Bankstown Remote Operations Centre capability was operating, staff had been trained, operating procedures and data-integration work had been carried out, and two capability-planning procurement instruments and DJI supplier relationships were already in train.

This is distinct from AR-013's procurement-architecture finding and AR-019's platform-capability finding: those paths concern what the procurement instruments and platform themselves are, while this path concerns what has already been physically, financially and organisationally committed - the specific categories of resource a future stop-or-continue decision would need to account for or reverse. None of the ten categories checked (committed funding, installed infrastructure, Remote Operations Centre build, trained-staff count, training expenditure, CASA approval instruments, operating procedures, data-integration work, procurement work, and supplier relationships) has a complete public figure or document; each is at best partially disclosed.
determinations: A material sunk-cost base already existed prior to completion of any Moree trial evaluation - operational infrastructure, a linked Remote Operations Centre capability, trained staff, in-train procurement instruments and DJI supplier relationships - even though the specific committed dollar total is undisclosed.
None of the ten specific commitment categories checked has a complete public figure or governing document; each is at best partially disclosed.

This commitment inventory is distinct from AR-014's continuation-past-window finding and AR-013's procurement-architecture finding: it names the actual categories of resource already committed that a future stop-or-continue decision would have to account for, rather than only the absence of stop criteria or the existence of separate procurement instruments.
mechanisms: The specific categories of already-committed resource - infrastructure, staffing, Remote Operations Centre capability, procurement instruments, supplier relationships - are established even though their financial scale is not; this is the concrete substrate AR-014's more general ratchet finding describes.
paths.boundary: No determination is made about the total financial value of commitments already made, or that any specific commitment was improper; the finding is limited to which categories of commitment already exist prior to evaluation completion and which of them remain undisclosed in scale.

paths.title: Evaluation-as-Precondition Gap and the Undefined Withdrawal Threshold
analysis: Section L of the same register (Q324-Q337) turns from what has already been committed (AR-052) to what, if anything, governs further commitment. No public document identifies pre-existing dock locations for a Mid North Coast rollout or completed engineering/coverage planning specific to Kempsey or the wider region - AR-002 already establishes that political contemplation of Kempsey as an expansion site predates the petition, but contemplation is not the same proposition as completed operational planning, which remains unestablished. Which existing commitments could be cancelled at negligible cost, which would carry significant termination cost, which infrastructure could be repurposed, and which contracts would continue regardless of trial outcome are all undetermined, because the underlying contract, asset and cost documents have not been acquired.

The section's most consequential finding is that no public rule makes completion of the Moree trial evaluation - whose existence, evaluator, design and publication commitment AR-026 through AR-031 already establish are all unattributed - a precondition for executing a new expansion contract, installing new docks, expanding operator recruitment or training, or expanding Remote Operations Centre capacity. On the current public record, none of these four forward steps is formally gated by that evaluation process. No explicit sunk-cost safeguard in the decision process has been publicly located either, and the specific point at which withdrawal would become operationally or politically difficult is an identifiable analytical question - not a currently measurable public fact.
determinations: No public document identifies pre-existing dock locations for a Mid North Coast rollout or completed engineering/coverage planning specific to Kempsey or the wider region, distinguishing political contemplation of expansion (established by AR-002 as predating the petition) from completed operational planning (not established).

Which existing commitments could be cancelled at negligible cost, which would carry significant termination cost, which infrastructure could be repurposed, and which contracts would continue regardless of trial outcome are all undetermined in the public record, because the underlying contract, asset and cost documents have not been acquired.

No public rule makes completion of the Moree trial evaluation a precondition for executing a new expansion contract, installing new docks, expanding operator recruitment or training, or expanding Remote Operations Centre capacity - none of these four forward steps is formally gated by the evaluation process AR-026 through AR-031 already establish has no named evaluator, design, or publication commitment.

No explicit sunk-cost safeguard in the decision process has been publicly located, and the specific threshold at which withdrawal would become operationally or politically difficult is an identified analytical question rather than a currently measurable public fact.
mechanisms: CONFIRMED: EVALUATION NOT A FORMAL GATE

Because no public rule requires the trial evaluation's completion before further contracts, docks, recruitment or Remote Operations Centre capacity expansion, the institutional path toward expansion can advance independent of whether the assessment process AR-026 through AR-031 describe as itself unattributed and undated ever concludes.
paths.boundary: No determination is made that NSW Police intends to expand before completing an evaluation, or that any specific forward step is already planned; only that no public rule requires the evaluation to precede any of the four forward steps checked, and that the withdrawal-difficulty threshold is an identified analytical question rather than a measured fact.

paths.title: Formal Decision-Making Authority and Approval-Gate Architecture Undisclosed
analysis: Section M of answer-register-l-to-t-run001.txt (Q338-Q363) turns from what has already been committed (AR-052) and what governs further commitment in the abstract (AR-053) to who specifically holds decision authority and which formal approvals a continuation or expansion decision would need to pass through. No public instrument has been located identifying the legal officer or body with final authority over whether PolAir-Remote continues, whether it expands, or where it expands; the Police Commissioner's general command and management responsibilities are documented, but no PolAir-Remote-specific instrument establishes that the Commissioner alone is the specific stop/go authority for this program, as distinct from a broader command structure that might require ministerial, Treasury, Cabinet, or standard procurement sign-off depending on the arrangement chosen.

A second, distinct cluster concerns which formal approval gates apply irrespective of who holds ultimate authority. AR-047 already established that no public AI Assessment Framework determination has been located for PolAir-Remote (a finding EV-0608/Q346 restates almost verbatim and is left unanchored here rather than duplicated), but this section's remaining approval questions are broader than that biometric-specific gap and have not previously been addressed: whether a Privacy Impact Assessment is required for the program generally (as distinct from AR-047.2's narrower finding that no PIA considering biometric linkage specifically has been located), whether a cyber-security accreditation or authority-to-operate is a required precondition (as distinct from AR-049's finding that specific security-assurance steps have not been shown to have been conducted), and whether CASA approval requirements vary by regional operating model, are each undisclosed or only partially established on the public record checked.
determinations: No public instrument identifies the specific legal officer or body with final authority over PolAir-Remote's continuation, expansion, or regional site-selection decisions, and none confirms whether the Police Commissioner alone holds that authority as distinct from a structure requiring further sign-off.
Whether ministerial, Treasury, Cabinet, or standard government-procurement approval is a required gate for continuation or expansion is undisclosed in the public record checked.

Whether a general Privacy Impact Assessment and a cyber-security accreditation/authority-to-operate are mandatory preconditions for this program, and whether CASA approval requirements vary by regional operating model, are each undisclosed or only partially established - distinct from AR-047's narrower biometric-specific PIA finding and AR-049's narrower conducted-steps finding.
mechanisms: Neither the identity of the decision-maker(s) for continuation, expansion, or site selection, nor the full set of approval gates (ministerial, Treasury, Cabinet, procurement, privacy, cyber-security, aviation) those decisions would need to pass through, is publicly reconstructable from any source located.
paths.boundary: No determination is made about who in fact holds decision authority, or that no internal approval process exists; only that no public instrument identifies the decision-maker(s) or confirms which formal approval gates apply to a continuation or expansion decision.

paths.title: Decision Thresholds, Triggers, and Stop/Go Record Status Undisclosed
analysis: The remainder of Section M (Q350-Q363) turns from who decides and what approvals apply (AR-054) to what evidentiary thresholds a decision would be measured against, and whether a decision has, in fact, already been made and recorded. No documentary checklist, performance threshold, cost-effectiveness threshold, privacy threshold, complaint threshold, or demographic-impact threshold has been publicly located for any pre-expansion or continuation decision. No published criterion for refusing expansion, modifying the existing deployment, or terminating the program has been located either; read alongside AR-014.2's existing general finding that no public stop, failure, or decommissioning criteria exist for this program, these three items extend that absence to each of the specific refusal, modification, and termination decision points individually, rather than restating it.

Separately, no formal public stop/go decision date, written decision record, or publication commitment for such a record has been located. AR-014.1 already establishes that operational use continued past the stated six-month trial window with no located extension notice; this section adds that continuation in practice does not itself establish that a formal permanent-expansion decision has occurred, been recorded in writing, or would be published if it had. Because no predefined public threshold of any of the five kinds checked has been located, the basis on which decision-makers would determine whether the trial "worked" is not publicly disclosed - the formal evaluation framework and business case AR-026 through AR-031 already establish are themselves unattributed remain the primary record that would resolve this.
determinations: No documentary checklist, performance threshold, cost-effectiveness threshold, privacy threshold, complaint threshold, or demographic-impact threshold has been publicly located for a pre-expansion or continuation decision.

No published criterion for refusing expansion, modifying the existing deployment, or terminating the program has been located, extending AR-014.2's general absent-exit-criteria finding to each of these three specific decision-trigger categories individually.

No formal public stop/go decision date, written decision record, or publication commitment for such a record has been located; continued operational use past the stated six-month window (AR-014.1) shows continuation in practice but does not establish that a formal permanent-expansion decision has occurred.
Because no predefined public threshold has been located, the basis on which decision-makers would determine whether the trial "worked" is not publicly disclosed.
mechanisms: Neither the thresholds a stop/go or expansion decision would be measured against, nor confirmation that any such formal decision has occurred, been recorded in writing, or would be published, is publicly reconstructable from any source located.
paths.boundary: No determination is made that NSW Police lacks internal thresholds or a decision record; only that none is publicly disclosed, so the basis for any future stop/go or expansion decision cannot currently be independently verified.

paths.title: Decommissioning Mechanics: Planning, Failure Response, and Asset/Access/Data Wind-Down
analysis: Section N, "Decommissioning and Exit Architecture" (Q364-Q379), turns from whether a stop/go decision exists at all (AR-014, AR-055) to what would concretely happen if one occurred. No pre-deployment decommissioning plan and no public failure-response plan specifying what must happen if the trial is judged unsuccessful have been publicly located. Nor has any public rule been located establishing whether Moree docks would be removed, whether aircraft would be reassigned, stored or disposed of, how software, cloud, or Remote Operations Centre access would be terminated, or whether operator permissions would be revoked.

The same gap extends to what happens to what the program has already collected and produced: no PolAir-specific deletion rule for stored imagery has been located (general records/disclosure obligations may separately require preservation in some cases), and while CASA aviation records carry substantial retention obligations in general, the specific treatment of PolAir telemetry after program termination is not public. No withdrawal process for operating procedures has been located, and whether the Remote Operations Centre would retain the technical ability to reactivate Moree capability after a termination is a governance/contract question not publicly resolved by anything located.
determinations: No pre-deployment decommissioning plan and no public failure-response plan for an unsuccessful trial outcome have been publicly located.

No public rule establishes whether docks would be removed, aircraft reassigned/stored/disposed of, software/cloud/Remote Operations Centre access terminated, or operator permissions revoked on termination.
No PolAir-specific deletion rule for stored imagery, and no public rule on post-termination treatment of telemetry records beyond CASA's general retention obligations, has been located.

No withdrawal process for operating procedures has been located, and whether the Remote Operations Centre would retain the technical ability to reactivate Moree capability after termination is unresolved on the public record.

This extends AR-014.2's general absent-exit-criteria finding to a distinct layer: not only are there no located criteria for deciding to stop the program, there is also no located rule for what would happen to its assets, access, or collected data if it did.
mechanisms: None of the ten specific asset, access, or data wind-down mechanics checked for a Moree termination scenario is publicly documented.
paths.boundary: No determination is made that NSW Police lacks internal decommissioning procedures; only that none is publicly disclosed, so a Mid North Coast rollout's own exit mechanics cannot currently be independently verified.

paths.title: Permanent-Capability Conversion Authority and Post-Termination Accountability
analysis: The remaining Section N items (Q374-Q379) turn from wind-down mechanics (AR-056) to two further, distinct gaps: the authority governing a shift from trial to permanent status, and the public accountability that would attach to a termination decision either way. Operational continuation beyond the nominal six-month window (AR-014.1) already shows that trial infrastructure can remain in use in practice; it does not establish whether converting that infrastructure into ordinary permanent police capability requires a distinct approval, and no public transition-authority instrument identifying who would make that call has been located.

Separately, whether existing contracts governing the Moree deployment are terminable without penalty is unknown because the relevant contracts have not been acquired - a different question from AR-050.2's finding that eighteen specific terms of a possible future RPAS panel contract, including its own exit-rights and data-return clauses, are undisclosed; AR-057 concerns the actual current deployment's own termination terms, not a prospective panel contract's undisclosed content. General NSW Government asset-disposal rules exist, but the applicable ownership/disposal path for Moree hardware specifically cannot be determined without the underlying asset and contract records. No public-notice requirement specific to PolAir-Remote termination, and no requirement compelling NSW Police to publish its reasons for terminating the capability, has been located either.
determinations: Whether converting trial infrastructure into ordinary permanent police capability requires a distinct approval, and who would hold authority over that transition, is not established by anything located.

Whether contracts governing the current Moree deployment are terminable without penalty is unknown because the relevant contracts have not been acquired - distinct from AR-050.2's finding about an undisclosed future RPAS panel contract's own exit-rights term.
The applicable ownership/disposal path for Moree hardware cannot be determined from general NSW Government asset-disposal rules alone, without the underlying asset and contract records.
No public-notice requirement for PolAir-Remote termination, and no requirement to publish the reasons for terminating it, has been located.
mechanisms: Neither the authority governing a trial-to-permanent conversion nor the public accountability that would attach to a termination decision is publicly reconstructable from any source located.
paths.boundary: No determination is made that NSW Police lacks an internal transition-authority instrument or disposal process; only that none is publicly disclosed, so neither a conversion-to-permanent decision nor a termination decision is currently publicly accountable.

paths.title: Consultation Content: Operational Disclosure Without Data-Architecture Disclosure
analysis: Two distinct Moree consultation events are on the public record: an 8 January 2026 briefing held the day the trial was reported to commence, and a separate formal "Have Your Say" process that closed 12 June 2026. Public reporting of what participants were told across both events - a six-month trial, remote operation, proactive flying, and covert/overt aerial exercises - concerns what the drone would visibly and operationally do. Two of those specific operational facts (proactive patrol, covert/overt exercises) are independently confirmed as disclosed by January reporting itself.

What is not established is disclosure of the data-handling architecture behind those operations. No record has been located showing that onboard AI or object-detection capability, retention arrangements, or the actual NSW Police data-hosting architecture were disclosed to participants at either event, and what recording policy (if any) was communicated to participants remains unresolved - later launch messaging describes a "not ordinarily recorded unless responding to crime" policy, but whether or how that was conveyed to consultation participants themselves is not established. This is a distinct gap from AR-015's sequencing finding (that consultation followed rather than preceded deployment): even considered on its own terms, independent of timing, the content of what was disclosed does not extend to the architecture governing what happens to collected data.
determinations: Public reporting of both Moree consultation events establishes disclosure of the drone's visible operational activity (a six-month trial, remote operation, proactive patrol, covert/overt exercises), independent of AR-015's separate finding about consultation's timing relative to deployment.

No public record establishes that onboard AI/object-detection capability, data-retention arrangements, or the NSW Police data-hosting architecture were disclosed to participants at either consultation event.

What recording policy, if any, was disclosed to participants remains unresolved: the only located recording-policy statement is later launch messaging that postdates both consultation events, and whether or how it was communicated to participants themselves is not established.
mechanisms: What a system visibly does (flies, patrols, records footage of an incident) is disclosed; what governs the data once collected (AI processing, retention, hosting) is not shown to have been. This is a content-of-disclosure pattern, distinct from a timing-of-disclosure pattern.
paths.boundary: No determination is made that briefing or consultation materials not publicly obtained omit this content, nor that any omission was deliberate; the finding is limited to what is publicly located as having been disclosed.

paths.title: Consultation's Absent Binding Authority and Accountability-Response Loop
analysis: Beyond timing (AR-015) and content (AR-058), the register shows a further, structurally distinct gap: no public record establishes that Moree consultation - at either the January briefing or the June "Have Your Say" process - carried binding authority over any of the specific operational parameters checked (limiting proactive patrol, altering retention settings, prohibiting particular analytics). The official consultation was framed as informing "future training, policy and capability development," language consistent with an advisory rather than binding process, though the register does not establish whether that limitation was itself disclosed to participants as a constraint on what their input could achieve.

A separate, related gap concerns accountability for the concerns that were raised. Privacy, mistrust, and safeguards concerns are independently documented as having been raised by the Aboriginal Legal Service and rights advocates, but no public record shows what happened to them afterward: no consultation-response matrix, no consolidated results document, no record of which proposed changes were rejected or why, and no record that feedback was ever supplied back to participants. A process can be genuinely advisory without being accountable for its own inputs; this section shows neither binding authority nor a visible accountability loop has been publicly established for either Moree consultation event.
determinations: No public record establishes that any Moree consultation process carried binding authority over the specific operational parameters checked: proactive-patrol scope, data-retention settings, or permitted analytics types.

Concerns raised through consultation (privacy, mistrust, safeguards) have no located public response: no response matrix, no consolidated results document, no record of rejected proposals or reasons for rejection, and no record that feedback was supplied back to participants.

The official framing of consultation as informing "future training, policy and capability development" is consistent with an advisory rather than binding process, though whether that limitation was itself disclosed to participants is not established.
mechanisms: Extends AR-015's same-named entry: beyond consultation following rather than preceding deployment, no binding authority over operational parameters and no visible response loop for raised concerns is publicly established either - two further, independent dimensions on which a consultation process could be genuine or performative, both currently unresolved on the public record.
paths.boundary: No determination is made that any specific concern was deliberately ignored, or that a response was withheld rather than never created; only that no such response record has been publicly located. No determination is made that the consultation process was conducted in bad faith.

paths.title: Kempsey-Specific Forward Consultation Commitments Undisclosed
analysis: The section's final four items turn from the Moree retrospective (AR-058, AR-059) to forward-looking questions specific to any Mid North Coast rollout. No commitment has been located requiring Kempsey consultation before deployment, nor before procurement or site selection specifically. No record establishes that Kempsey residents would hold a binding choice over whether deployment occurs at all, and no public rule requires consultation to be repeated should the deployed technical capability materially change after any rollout begins.

Read against AR-015's and AR-058/AR-059's Moree findings - consultation that followed deployment, disclosed operational but not data-architecture content, and carried no established binding authority or response loop - the absence of any forward commitment specific to Kempsey means the Moree pattern is, on the current public record, the only available precedent for what a Kempsey process would look like. This is a description of what is currently undisclosed, not a prediction of what will occur.
determinations: No public commitment requires Kempsey-specific consultation before deployment, before procurement, or before site selection.
No public record establishes that Kempsey residents would hold a binding choice over whether deployment occurs at all.
No public rule requires consultation to be repeated should the deployed technical capability materially change after any Kempsey rollout begins.
paths.boundary: No determination is made that Kempsey consultation will not occur or will necessarily replicate the Moree pattern; the finding is limited to the absence of any currently located public commitment governing it.

paths.title: Moree Youth Crime Governance Group: No Located Oversight Function Beyond Consultation, Approval, or Co-Design
analysis: AR-015 already establishes that no public record shows the Moree Youth Crime Governance Group was formally consulted, gave approval, or held co-design input before PolAir-Remote deployment; the section's next eight items were checked against that existing finding before being treated as new (Q406-Q408/EV-0668-EV-0670 restate the same three-part claim almost verbatim and are left unanchored for that reason, consistent with the discipline DEC-0009/DEC-0010 established). What those items add beyond AR-015's consultation/approval/co-design finding is a further, distinct set of ongoing oversight functions: no record shows the Governance Group set the trial's success criteria, set surveillance boundaries, or reviewed its privacy safeguards or a privacy impact assessment; and no record shows it received the trial's formal performance dataset/evaluation, or currently receives flight-level or outcome reporting.
