A separate strand within the same section concerns three organisations independently confirmed as represented within the Governance Group's broader membership: Moree Local Aboriginal Land Council co-chairs the Group, the Aboriginal Legal Service's regional manager attended the January 2026 drone briefing, and Aboriginal community-controlled organisations more generally are described as strongly represented in Moree's broader youth-crime governance. None of the three is shown to hold a further, PolAir-Remote-specific operational-review or oversight authority distinct from that general membership. This refines rather than repeats AR-015.2's finding that no ACCO consultation, approval, or co-design is established: general representation within a relevant body is shown here for the first time, alongside the continued absence of any program-specific authority attached to it.
determinations: No public record shows the Moree Youth Crime Governance Group set PolAir-Remote's trial success criteria, set surveillance boundaries, or reviewed its privacy safeguards or a privacy impact assessment.
No public record shows the Governance Group received PolAir-Remote's formal trial performance dataset or evaluation, or currently receives flight-level or outcome reporting.

Moree Local Aboriginal Land Council, the Aboriginal Legal Service, and Aboriginal community-controlled organisations more generally are each independently confirmed as represented within the Governance Group's broader youth-crime governance role; none is shown to hold a further, PolAir-Remote-specific operational-review or oversight authority distinct from that general membership.
paths.boundary: No determination is made that the Governance Group was deliberately excluded from these functions, or that it sought and was refused such a role; only that no public record locates it holding them. No determination is made about whether LALC, ALS, or ACCO representatives raised PolAir-specific concerns through a channel not captured by this register. Q406-Q408/EV-0668-EV-0670 are intentionally left unanchored as a restatement of AR-015's existing consultation/approval/co-design finding, not as an omission.

paths.title: Kempsey Reference Group: Existing Body, No Located Forward Authority Over PolAir Deployment
analysis: Kempsey has an existing Reference Group, distinct from Moree's Youth Crime Governance Group, that includes NSW Police and Aboriginal community-controlled organisations and co-develops the area's youth-crime Action Plan. No record commits that Group to review a PolAir-Remote proposal before deployment, and no document establishes that it could recommend against deployment or impose binding operational conditions on NSW Police. No commitment has been located to provide it with continuing flight or outcome data, and no requirement has been located compelling NSW Police to respond publicly to any recommendation it made.

Read against AR-060's finding that no Kempsey-specific consultation commitment exists before deployment, procurement, or site selection, this establishes a second, distinct gap at Kempsey: even where an existing local body with relevant standing already exists, no record establishes that it holds a review, veto, conditions-setting, data-access, or public-accountability function over a prospective PolAir rollout specifically.
determinations: Kempsey's existing Reference Group is confirmed to include NSW Police and Aboriginal community-controlled organisations and to co-develop the area's youth-crime Action Plan, distinct from Moree's Youth Crime Governance Group.
No record commits the Kempsey Reference Group to review a PolAir-Remote proposal before deployment, or establishes that it could recommend against deployment or impose binding operational conditions.

No commitment has been located to provide the Kempsey Reference Group with continuing PolAir-Remote flight or outcome data, and no requirement has been located compelling NSW Police to respond publicly to any recommendation it made.
paths.boundary: No determination is made that the Reference Group has sought such a role and been refused, or that no informal channel for input exists; only that no public record establishes these specific functions. No determination is made about what function, if any, the Group will hold once a Kempsey-specific proposal is made public.

paths.title: Aboriginal Processing-Funnel Disproportionality: Unmeasurable Absent Person-Level Data
analysis: Section Q (Q423-Q433) checks eleven distinct stages of PolAir-Remote-associated processing for Aboriginal-specific disproportionality: the proportion of flights over high-Aboriginal-population areas, and the proportion of persons tracked, stopped following drone detection, arrested, charged, who are children, placed on bail, refused bail, entering remand, receiving diversion, or experiencing repeat drone-associated police contact. No de-identified Moree mission/person-level demographic dataset covering any of these eleven stages has been published or acquired, so none of the requested proportions can presently be calculated. This is a distinct scope from AR-039's existing finding: AR-039 (Section E) concerns only spatial/flight-geography exposure - whether the aerial footprint itself falls disproportionately on an area - while this section concerns the full downstream criminal-justice processing funnel from initial tracking through to diversion outcome, which AR-039 does not reach.

The section's four analytical follow-up questions (Q434-Q437) show the gap compounds rather than standing alone: local Aboriginal population share is itself publicly available, but cannot be turned into a meaningful exposure or contact-rate comparison without the stage-specific numerators Q423-Q433 seek; testing whether any disparity is explained by underlying offending patterns requires offence-involvement, location, tasking-mode, time and repeat-contact data linked at the person level, which is not available; and testing whether disparities differ between proactive and reactive taskings requires mission classification joined to demographic exposure data, which likewise does not exist in the public record. This is distinct from AR-024.3's existing finding that BOCSAR's evaluation of the Suspect Target Management Plan - a different NSW Police program - found a smaller associated offending reduction for Aboriginal people alongside a larger associated increase in imprisonment risk: that finding establishes comparable disparities are criminologically plausible for a targeted-policing program, not that they have or have not occurred within PolAir-Remote's own processing funnel specifically.
determinations: No de-identified Moree mission/person-level demographic dataset establishing the proportion of PolAir-Remote flights over high-Aboriginal-population areas, or the proportion of persons tracked, stopped following drone detection, arrested, charged, or who are children, has been published or acquired.

No dataset establishing the proportion of Aboriginal people placed on bail, refused bail, entering remand, receiving diversion, or experiencing repeat drone-associated police contact has been published or acquired.

Because the stage-specific numerators in AR-063.1/AR-063.2 are unavailable, they cannot presently be compared against local Aboriginal population share, tested against underlying offence involvement, or tested for whether disparities differ between proactive and reactive taskings - each of these three analytical questions is compounded by, not independent of, the absence of the underlying processing-funnel data.

This extends AR-039's flight-geography-only disproportionality gap (Section E) to the full downstream processing funnel from initial tracking through diversion outcome; it is a distinct scope, not a repeat, of AR-039's spatial-exposure finding.
mechanisms: The absence of any de-identified mission/person-level dataset prevents independent testing of Aboriginal processing-funnel disproportionality at any of the eleven stages checked; this does not establish that disproportionate impact exists, only that it cannot currently be tested.
paths.boundary: No determination is made that PolAir-Remote's processing funnel is or is not disproportionate for Aboriginal people at any of the eleven stages checked; only that the public record does not currently contain the person-level data that would be needed to test this either way.

paths.title: Closing the Gap Alignment and Evaluation-KPI Gap: Targets 10/11 and ACCO Data Access
analysis: Q438-Q440 ask whether a Closing the Gap impact assessment has been conducted for PolAir-Remote, and whether any evaluation tests the program's implications for National Agreement on Closing the Gap Target 10 (reducing adult incarceration) or Target 11 (reducing youth detention) specifically. None of the three has been publicly located. This is distinct from AR-030's existing, broader finding: AR-030 (Q36-Q44) established that demographic impact and Aboriginal justice-system contact are not shown to be measured at all as general trial outcomes; this section asks the more specific question of whether any such measurement, if it existed, would be tested against the Closing the Gap National Agreement's own named targets - a policy-framework alignment question AR-030's source material did not itself ask.

Q441-Q443 extend the same undisclosed-evaluation-KPI gap to three further specific measures - community trust, willingness to report crime, and perceptions of over-surveillance - none shown to be a PolAir-Remote evaluation KPI in the public record checked. Q444 separately establishes that while the Closing the Gap framework supports shared Aboriginal-organisation access to locally relevant data as a general principle, no record establishes that Aboriginal organisations receive de-identified PolAir-Remote outcome data specifically. This refines rather than repeats AR-061.2's existing, narrower finding, which concerned only whether the Moree Youth Crime Governance Group specifically currently receives PolAir-Remote outcome reporting: this item asks the broader question of Aboriginal organisations generally, not only that one governance body.
determinations: No PolAir-Remote-specific Closing the Gap impact assessment, and no formal evaluation testing Target 10 (adult incarceration) or Target 11 (youth detention) implications, has been publicly located.
No evidence has been located showing community trust, willingness to report crime, or perceptions of over-surveillance are tracked as PolAir-Remote evaluation KPIs.

While the Closing the Gap framework supports shared Aboriginal-organisation access to locally relevant data as a general principle, no record establishes that Aboriginal organisations receive de-identified PolAir-Remote outcome data specifically - a broader question than AR-061.2's existing finding about one governance body's own outcome reporting.

This extends AR-030's general rights- and equity-metrics-undisclosed finding (Q36-Q44) to the specific Closing the Gap National Agreement targets and evaluation-KPI categories that source material did not itself name.
mechanisms: Absence of a public evaluation-KPI framework naming Closing the Gap Targets 10/11, community trust, willingness to report, or over-surveillance perceptions is consistent with either non-tracking or non-publication; the public record does not distinguish these.
paths.boundary: No determination is made that PolAir-Remote's evaluation, if one exists internally, omits Closing the Gap alignment or these KPIs - only that none is publicly disclosed. No determination is made that Aboriginal organisations have sought and been refused de-identified outcome data.

paths.title: Operation Soteria Original Cohort Identity, Composition, and Longitudinal Accounting Undisclosed
analysis: Section R (Q446-Q452) checks whether the original approximately 80-100 'ringleader' cohort NSW Police publicly named at Operation Soteria's launch - aged roughly 11-16 across nine northern/western regional hotspots - has ever been broken down and published as a tracked group in its own right. No per-location split (how many were in Moree, how many in Kempsey), no age-band split within the stated 11-16 range, no Aboriginality count, no pre-existing bail status at intake, and no specific person-level inclusion rule beyond the general offence-type description (serious repeat regional offending, particularly aggravated break-enter-steal, motor-vehicle theft, and post-and-boast/performance offending) has been publicly located. This is a narrower and prior question than AR-063's: AR-063 tests Aboriginal-specific disproportionality across all PolAir-Remote-associated processing generally; this section asks whether the one specific, officially-named target cohort itself - not PolAir-Remote's processing population at large - has ever been tracked or published as a defined group at all, a gap that would remain even if AR-063's population-wide data existed.

Section R (Q453-Q463) then checks whether that named cohort has ever been accounted for longitudinally. No count of original members who ceased offending, remain active, entered custody, completed diversion, or left the cohort for other reasons has been published or acquired, and no count of new entrants replacing them exists either. Because none of that person-level exit/entry data exists, none of the metrics that depend on it can presently be calculated from the public record: a current like-for-like cohort size, a replacement rate, a reoffending rate, an average number of legal actions per original member, or the proportion of published operational activity attributable to repeated processing of the same individuals. This compounds rather than merely restates AR-006's existing counterfactual-design gap: AR-006 identifies that no comparator design exists for testing PolAir-Remote's town-level effect; this section shows that even the most basic precondition for a person-level version of that design - a tracked identity for the specific cohort NSW Police itself named - was never established publicly in the first place.
determinations: No per-location breakdown (Moree, Kempsey) of the original approximately 80-100 Operation Soteria cohort has been publicly located or acquired.

No age-band, Aboriginality, or pre-existing bail-status breakdown of the original cohort, and no specific person-level inclusion rule beyond a general offence-type description, has been publicly located - a narrower and prior question than AR-063's population-wide Aboriginal processing-funnel finding, not a repeat of it.
No longitudinal accounting of original-cohort exits (ceased offending, entered custody, completed diversion, left for other reasons) or new entrants has been publicly located or acquired.

Because the person-level dataset AR-065.1-AR-065.3 identify as absent does not exist publicly, derived cohort metrics - current like-for-like cohort size, replacement rate, reoffending rate, average legal actions per member, and the proportion of activity attributable to repeat processing of the same individuals - cannot presently be calculated from the public record.
mechanisms: The absence of any public tracking of the specific, officially-named target cohort prevents independent testing of its composition or longitudinal outcomes; this does not establish that such tracking does not exist internally, only that none is publicly disclosed.
paths.boundary: No determination is made that the original Operation Soteria cohort is or is not tracked internally, or that its members have or have not desisted, been replaced, or reoffended at any particular rate - only that no public record establishes any of this either way.

paths.title: PolAir-Assisted Arrests Not Linked to Soteria Cohort Membership; Detection-versus-Reduction Mechanism Unmeasurable at Cohort Level
analysis: Section R's final items (Q464-Q469) ask whether PolAir-assisted arrests can be tied specifically to membership, or non-membership, of the original Operation Soteria cohort, and whether PolAir-Remote's effect on that cohort can be distinguished from mere increased detection of existing offending. No data link PolAir-assisted arrests to cohort membership in either direction, so this question cannot presently be answered from the public record.

AR-024 already establishes deterrence via increased perceived detection probability as a criminologically-plausible alternative to incapacitation for Moree's aggregate town-level decline, and separately notes no public evaluation measures the perceived-certainty variables that hypothesis requires. This section shows the same detection-versus-reduction distinction is also untestable at the more specific, officially-named cohort level: even if the aggregate question were somehow resolved, whether PolAir-Remote reduces offending among cohort members specifically, alters the time between their offences, improves their diversion completion, or reduces their replacement by new entrants could not be determined, because - per AR-065 - no data links PolAir-assisted arrests to that cohort at all, and no longitudinal person-level record of the cohort exists to test against.
determinations: No data link PolAir-assisted arrests to membership, or non-membership, of the original Operation Soteria cohort.

Whether PolAir-Remote reduces offending specifically among cohort members, as distinct from merely increasing detection of their existing offending, cannot be determined from the public record - extending AR-024's aggregate-level deterrence-versus-detection question to the cohort-specific level, which requires the person-level linkage AR-065 already establishes is unavailable.

Whether PolAir-Remote alters the time between offences, improves diversion completion, or reduces replacement by new entrants for cohort members specifically cannot be determined from the public record.
mechanisms: Absence of any public linkage between PolAir-assisted arrests and the named target cohort prevents independent testing of whether the program reduces offending, alters offence timing, improves diversion, or reduces replacement for that cohort specifically; this does not establish the answer either way, only that it cannot presently be tested.
paths.boundary: No determination is made that PolAir-Remote does or does not reduce offending among Operation Soteria cohort members, alter inter-offence timing, improve diversion completion, or reduce replacement by new entrants - only that the public record lacks the cohort-linked data that would let any of this be tested.

paths.title: PolAir-Associated Bail-Interaction Outcomes: No Aggregate Accounting Published
analysis: Section S's first five items (Q470-Q474) ask for the plain aggregate count and outcome breakdown of PolAir-associated bail interactions - not disaggregated by any demographic characteristic, only totalled. Individual PolAir-associated cases visible in media releases (see SRC-0042's report of a 2 August 2026 domestic violence/bail matter) establish that bail breach allegations, bail refusals and remand outcomes do occur in connection with PolAir-associated arrests, but none of the five items locates a published total: how many PolAir-associated arrests involved a person already on bail, how many produced bail-breach allegations, how many resulted in bail refusal, how many resulted in remand, and how many involved technical breach rather than new substantive offending are each answered in the source register by individual example rather than aggregate count.

This is a plainer question than AR-063's existing finding. AR-063 establishes that no de-identified, person-level dataset covers the placed-on-bail, refused-bail or remand stages of PolAir-Remote's processing funnel, so Aboriginal-specific disproportionality at those stages cannot presently be tested. Section S shows the absence runs one level deeper: the plain, non-demographic aggregate those stages would need as their own denominator - before any demographic breakdown is even attempted - has not been published either, for anyone. A genuine cross-path convergence with AR-063 is recorded as CPO-024.
determinations: No aggregate count of PolAir-associated arrests involving a person already on bail has been published; individual cases establish the outcome occurs, but no denominator exists.

No aggregate count of PolAir-associated bail-breach allegations, bail refusals, or remand outcomes has been published - the same individual-example-without-total pattern recurs across all three outcome categories.

No dataset isolates whether a PolAir-associated bail-related outcome involved a technical breach as distinct from new substantive offending, so even an eventual aggregate could not presently be broken down by breach type.
mechanisms: Absence of any published aggregate for PolAir-associated bail-interaction outcomes prevents independent testing of the program's relationship to bail, breach and remand outcomes at even the simplest, non-demographic level.
paths.boundary: No determination is made about how many PolAir-associated arrests actually involved bail breach, refusal, or remand, or what proportion were technical rather than substantive; only that no published aggregate answers these questions, at either the plain or demographically-disaggregated level.

paths.title: Undisclosed Authorisation Pathway for Extending PolAir-Remote Into Bail, ADVO, and Judicial-Supervision Compliance Monitoring
analysis: Section S's middle items (Q475-Q477) test whether PolAir-Remote's role in judicial-supervision compliance work is limited to incidental presence during broader operations or extends to dedicated tasking. No evidence establishes that a PolAir-Remote mission has ever been specifically tasked to monitor bail compliance as its primary purpose (Q475). At the same time, the register's own PARTIAL classifications for Q476-Q477 establish that PolAir-Remote has been deployed during Operation Soteria surge activity in which officers conducted bail-compliance checks, and has been present during operations containing ADVO-compliance checks, without evidence that the drone itself performed either check. This leaves current use in an undocumented intermediate position - present during compliance-monitoring operations, but not shown to be a dedicated compliance-monitoring tool in its own right - and the source material identifies no policy drawing or governing that line.

Section S's next items (Q478-Q481) ask whether the same capability could be extended to curfew-compliance monitoring or to locating electronically monitored persons, and what authorisation such an extension would require. The controlling RPAS/bail-monitoring policy is not public, so neither permissibility nor governing conditions for either use can currently be established, and no operational example of either use has been located. This is a distinct gap from AR-047's biometric-authorisation-pathway finding: AR-047 concerns whether captured imagery can be matched against a person's identity, while this section concerns whether the platform's surveillance function itself can be redirected toward monitoring compliance with a court-imposed condition (bail, curfew, an electronic-monitoring order) rather than detecting new offending - a different extension of the same undisclosed-authorisation-pathway problem.

Section S's closing analytical items (Q482-Q483) ask what demographic impact such an extension would create and how it would interact with Closing the Gap targets. Modelling either requires data on who would be monitored, baseline bail/justice contact rates, and false or secondary detection rates and their resulting custody effects - none of which is available for the platform's current use, let alone a hypothetical extension into dedicated compliance-monitoring tasking - so neither question can presently be answered from the public record.
determinations: No evidence establishes that a PolAir-Remote mission has been specifically tasked to monitor bail compliance as a primary purpose, though the platform has been present during Operation Soteria surge operations and operations containing ADVO-compliance checks without evidence that it performed those checks itself.

The policy governing whether PolAir-Remote could be used for curfew-compliance monitoring or to locate electronically monitored persons, and what separate authorisation any such use would require, is not public.

The demographic impact of extending PolAir-Remote into dedicated technological bail-compliance monitoring, and its interaction with the Closing the Gap National Agreement's Target 11, cannot be determined from the public record absent baseline bail/justice-contact and detection-rate data that do not currently exist.
mechanisms: Absence of a public policy governing extension of PolAir-Remote's surveillance function to bail, curfew, or electronic-monitoring compliance leaves the boundary between incidental presence and dedicated tasking undocumented and unauditable.
paths.boundary: No determination is made that PolAir-Remote has been tasked, formally or informally, to monitor bail, ADVO, or curfew compliance, or that any authorisation for such use does or does not exist internally; only that no public record establishes dedicated tasking for that purpose, the policy that would govern an extension to it, or the demographic effect such an extension would have.

paths.title: Nine Individually Named Moree System Cost Components Have No Published Figure At All
analysis: AR-005 already establishes that no complete drone-system cost numerator is publicly available, and AR-033 already establishes that none of eight cost components is confirmed included or excluded from the petition's helicopter-cost comparison. Section T of the Continuing Investigation Question Bank Answer Register (Q485-Q493) establishes a more basic gap beneath both: for nine individually named cost categories - recurrent cost, annual operator cost, annual Remote Operations Centre cost, maintenance cost, communications cost, software/licensing cost, regulatory-compliance cost, data-storage cost, and training cost - no public figure of any kind has been located, for either side of any comparison. This is not a boundary-definition problem (AR-033's question of what is included or excluded) or an aggregate-numerator problem (AR-005's question of what the total is); it is the prior question of whether each individual line item exists in public form at all, and for all nine checked, it does not.

AR-052 separately establishes that a real, multi-category commitment base - installed infrastructure, a linked Remote Operations Centre, trained staff, in-train procurement instruments and supplier relationships - existed before any trial evaluation was completed, without a complete public dollar figure for any category. This path is the direct cost-disclosure counterpart to that commitment inventory: AR-052 asks what has been committed in kind; this path asks what has been costed in dollars for the same kind of categories, and finds neither published for any of the nine checked.
determinations: None of nine individually named Moree system cost categories - recurrent, operator, Remote Operations Centre, maintenance, communications, software/licensing, regulatory-compliance, data-storage, and training - has a published dollar figure.

This is a more basic gap than AR-033's finding that these categories are not confirmed included or excluded from the petition's cost comparison, and distinct from AR-052's finding that the underlying commitments exist without a dollar figure: this path establishes the dollar figures themselves are absent for each category, independent of any comparison or commitment question.
Absent any of these nine figures, neither AR-005's called-for complete drone-system cost numerator nor AR-033's inclusion/exclusion boundary can be constructed even in principle.
mechanisms: Nine individually named cost categories that a complete system-cost numerator would need to sum have no published figure at all, not merely an unresolved comparison boundary.
paths.boundary: No determination is made about the actual scale of any of these nine cost categories, or that their non-publication is deliberate; only that none has been publicly located as at this pass.

paths.title: Thirteen Derived Cost and Workload Metrics the Program's Net Economic Effect Would Require Cannot Presently Be Calculated
analysis: AR-018 already establishes that no public evaluation integrates PolAir-Remote's system cost with downstream justice-system cost and prevented-harm benefit in a single net-cost model. Section T's Q494-Q506 name the specific derived metrics such a model would require and confirm each is presently uncalculable: cost per flight, per operational deployment, per successful location, per vehicle recovery attributable to the system, and per missing-person outcome each depend on a verified cost figure (absent per AR-069) and a verified, mission-classified activity count, neither currently linked in public data; cost per officer-hour saved additionally requires a time-and-motion or tasking dataset that has not been published; and the number of conventional PolAir hours displaced, and any resulting monetary saving, cannot be calculated without a verified displacement count.

The same section separately establishes that five categories of downstream justice-system workload PolAir-Remote's own detections may generate - additional ground-police dispatch and follow-up work, custody workload, court workload, Legal Aid workload, and bail-supervision workload - have no linked mission-to-outcome dataset published for any of them. This gives AR-018's general downstream-cost-multiplier finding its specific missing components: it is not only that no single integrated model exists, but that none of the five workload categories that model would need to sum has itself been separately quantified.
determinations: Six derived unit-cost metrics (cost per flight, per operational deployment, per successful location, per vehicle recovery, per missing-person outcome, and per officer-hour saved) cannot presently be calculated, each for want of a verified cost figure, a verified mission-classified activity count, or both.
Neither the number of conventional PolAir hours displaced by PolAir-Remote nor any resulting monetary saving has been publicly quantified.

Five categories of downstream justice-system workload potentially generated by PolAir-Remote's own detections - ground-police, custody, court, Legal Aid, and bail-supervision workload - have no linked mission-to-outcome dataset published for any of them, giving AR-018's general downstream-cost-multiplier finding its specific missing components.
mechanisms: Thirteen named derived metrics a net-economic-effect model would require - unit costs and downstream workload categories alike - are each individually uncalculated, not merely unintegrated into one model.
paths.boundary: No determination is made about what any of these metrics would show if calculated, or that displaced hours or generated workload are large or small in scale; only that none of the thirteen derived metrics checked has been publicly quantified as at this pass.

paths.title: The Benefit Side and Every Named Investment Alternative Remain Unquantified, Leaving Marginal Yield Undetermined
analysis: Section T's Q507-Q511 test whether the benefit side of a net-cost-per-prevented-harm calculation is any more available than the cost side AR-069 and AR-070 establish is missing. It is not: no linked dataset totals detention expenditure following PolAir-associated arrests (against the register's own benchmark of $2,573.26 per young person per day in youth detention versus $367.68 for community supervision, itself a general system-cost differential, not attributable PolAir expenditure); no formal Moree evaluation quantifies victim harm avoided, distinguishing plausible benefit visible in individual tactical outcomes from a monetised figure; and no verified aggregate exists for property value recovered, dangerous pursuits avoided, or search-and-rescue costs avoided.

Q513-Q515 and Q517-Q518 test the claim's remaining implicit comparison base by asking how PolAir-Remote compares with five specific policy alternatives named in the case's own material: frontline police staffing, youth intervention programs (against which Kempsey's $3.8 million place-based investment and the $934,725 five-year Kempsey Casework Support Program contract are named as scale comparators, not proof of relative outcome), fixed CCTV (already substantially deployed in Kempsey), improved bail support (against the $8.75 million Moree bail accommodation/support program and later intensive bail support), and community supervision (against the NSW Audit Office's own published $367.68-versus-$2,573.26 per-day differential, which establishes a justice-cost gap but not that supervision substitutes for a policing technology or prevents the same harms). No like-for-like comparison has been published against any of the five. A sixth comparison in the same run of questions, against conventional PolAir (Q516), was checked and found to restate AR-005.3's and AR-033's already-established helicopter-comparison-methodology gap, and is not treated as new here.

Q519's marginal-yield question - what is the marginal yield of the next dollar spent on PolAir-Remote versus these alternatives - is consequently not calculable: it would require the cost-side figures AR-069 and AR-070 establish are absent, the benefit-side figures this path establishes are equally absent, and a common prevented-harm/system-cost outcome measure across all five alternatives, none of which currently exists. Q512's own framing of 'net cost per prevented harm' as the correct evaluative unit was checked and found to restate AR-018.3's and AR-005.4's already-established determination, and is likewise not treated as new here.
determinations: No linked dataset quantifies detention expenditure following PolAir-associated arrests, victim harm avoided, property value recovered, dangerous pursuits avoided, or search-and-rescue costs avoided - the benefit side of a net-cost calculation is as unquantified as AR-069/AR-070 establish the cost side to be.

No like-for-like comparison has been published between PolAir-Remote and any of five named policy alternatives - frontline police staffing, youth intervention programs, fixed CCTV, improved bail support, or community supervision.

The marginal yield of the next dollar spent on PolAir-Remote against these alternatives is not calculable from the public record, absent both the cost-side figures AR-069/AR-070 establish are missing and the benefit-side figures this path establishes are equally missing.

Two items in this section - the net-cost-per-prevented-harm framing (Q512) and the comparison against conventional PolAir specifically (Q516) - were checked against AR-018.3/AR-005.4 and AR-005.3/AR-033 respectively, found to restate those already-established determinations, and are not anchored to this or any new path.
mechanisms: The benefit side of the net-cost-per-prevented-harm calculation, and every named alternative-investment comparison, is as unpublished as the cost side AR-069/AR-070 establish, leaving the marginal-yield question unanswerable in practice rather than only undefined in principle.
paths.boundary: No determination is made about whether PolAir-Remote's benefit exceeds, matches, or falls short of any named alternative, or about the actual scale of any unquantified harm-avoided or cost-avoided figure; only that the public record does not currently support the comparison or the marginal-yield calculation Q519 asks for.

paths.title: Town-Level Site-Selection Correlation: A Structural Layer Prior to Flight-Geography and Processing-Funnel Exposure
analysis: Reading preserved/snapshot-03-2026-08-14.txt's Section 29 ("New Direction - Selection Effects and Aboriginal Community Impact") in full against this case's existing Aboriginal-disproportionality findings shows a distinct, prior layer neither AR-039 nor AR-063 reaches. Moree, Kempsey and Tamworth - the towns this case's own record identifies as targeted for enhanced regional youth-crime response, including Moree as PolAir-Remote's own host town - each carry an Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander population share above the NSW average. NSW Government publicly states the selection criterion for targeted intervention was comparatively higher youth-crime rates, not population composition, and no evidence located establishes population share as an intended or stated criterion.

AR-039 tests whether flight patterns within an already-selected town are geographically disproportionate relative to that town's own internal demographic distribution; AR-063 tests whether the downstream processing funnel from an already-operating deployment is disproportionate. Neither reaches the prior question this section raises: because a town-sited aerial capability necessarily inherits whatever demographic composition characterises its host town, population-level disproportionate exposure to a geographically-anchored capability is foreseeable from town selection alone, before any flight pattern or processing stage is examined - independent of whether that selection was itself demographically motivated.
determinations: Moree, Kempsey and Tamworth - the towns this case's own record identifies as targeted for enhanced regional policing/place-based youth-crime response, including Moree as PolAir-Remote's own host town - each carry an Aboriginal/Torres Strait Islander population share above the NSW average; NSW Government states the selection criterion was comparatively higher youth-crime rates, not population composition.
No evidence located establishes that Aboriginal population share was an intended or stated site-selection criterion for Moree, Kempsey or Tamworth's targeted policing/place-based programs.

Because a town-sited aerial capability inherits its host town's demographic composition regardless of how that town was selected, town-level selection is a structurally prior layer to both AR-039's within-town flight-geography question and AR-063's downstream processing-funnel question - distinct from, and not answered by, either.
paths.boundary: No determination is made that Moree, Kempsey or Tamworth's selection for targeted policing/place-based response was motivated by, or designed around, Aboriginal population share; only that the towns targeted for that response share this demographic characteristic above the state average, and that this is a distinct, prior layer to the flight-geography and processing-funnel disproportionality questions this case already tracks.

paths.title: Regional Network Architecture: Finite Node Coverage and the Design Inputs a Feasibility Study Would Require
analysis: AR-017 already establishes that the petition's 'Mid North Coast' wording does not specify a single-installation or multi-node rollout, and that no public feasibility or coverage study exists. Reading preserved/snapshot-10-2026-08-16.txt (Findings F-182 through F-184, F-197 through F-199) in full against AR-017 supplies the specific engineering reasons that gap matters and the specific inputs a genuine design study would need. Manufacturer material gives the Dock 3/Matrice 4-series platform a maximum test operating radius of around 10 km and a flight time of up to 54 minutes under specified conditions; distances from a West Kempsey installation to other Mid North Coast district centres are many multiples of that radius. A single fixed dock is therefore a local-coverage asset, not district-wide rapid-response coverage, regardless of where within Kempsey it is sited.

The platform supports vehicle-mounted deployment and multi-dock tasking, and reference-condition recharge (15% to 95%) takes about 27 minutes with no automatic battery swap, so genuine regional coverage would require a multi-node, mobile, or mixed architecture - combining fixed docks, mobile docks, conventional PolAir and existing ground/CCTV/MANPR capability - accounting for node density, concurrent demand and recharge downtime, rather than a single dock or a uniform 'dock per station' assumption. Responsibly specifying the number and location of nodes requires geocoded demand data, time-critical incident categories, terrain/communications modelling, CASA approvals and site-resilience assessment; none of these inputs, nor a study applying them, has been publicly located. Flood- and storm-related power/communications interruption is a legitimate site-selection factor given the platform's stable-power/internet dependency and a backup battery that does not charge the aircraft - the source material is explicit that this establishes a design factor, not a finding that any particular candidate site is itself flood-prone, and that limitation is preserved here rather than converted into a site-specific claim.
determinations: Manufacturer specification gives the Dock 3/Matrice 4-series platform a maximum test operating radius of approximately 10 km and a flight time of up to 54 minutes under specified conditions, establishing that a single fixed dock is a local-coverage asset, not district-wide coverage, wherever within Kempsey it is sited.

Genuine Mid North Coast coverage would require a multi-node, mobile, or mixed deployment architecture accounting for node density, concurrent demand and recharge downtime (approximately 27 minutes per reference-condition cycle, no automatic battery swap); no such design has been publicly documented.

Flood- and storm-related power/communications interruption is a legitimate site-selection factor given the platform's site-infrastructure dependency; no determination is made about whether any specific candidate site is itself flood-prone.

Responsible node-count and node-location specification requires geocoded demand data, response-time thresholds, terrain/communications modelling, CASA approvals and site-resilience assessment; none of these design inputs, nor a study applying them, has been publicly located - giving YIELD-REQ-006's existing request for a coverage/feasibility study the specific engineering basis for why it is a substantive requirement rather than a formality.
mechanisms: Absent a published design study, the petition's 'Mid North Coast' wording risks being read by signatories or decision-makers as implying multi-node district coverage, when the platform's own finite operating radius makes a single-dock reading technically insufficient regardless of where that dock is placed.
paths.boundary: No determination is made about how many nodes, of what type, would be needed for a responsible Mid North Coast rollout, about the appropriate site for any node, or about whether NSW Police intends a single-node or multi-node rollout (that remains undisclosed, per AR-017.2); only that no public study currently applies the necessary design inputs, and that the underlying platform's own finite operating radius makes a single-dock reading of 'Mid North Coast' insufficient by itself.

paths.title: DJI's Documented NSW Lobbying Footprint: Presence Established, Influence Over PolAir-Remote Not Established
analysis: The NSW Electoral Commission's lobbyist register lists 'DJI' among one active registered lobbyist's client records and 'DJI Technology Australia Pty. Ltd.' among a separate active registered lobbyist's client records. Electoral Commission guidance defines a client broadly as a third party that has retained or provided lobbying services directly or indirectly, and the register view aggregates current and historical client information rather than dating individual engagements - so this establishes a NSW lobbying footprint, not the specific dates or subject matter of any engagement.

No evidence located connects this registered lobbying activity to the Moree trial, Michael Kemp, Yasmin Catley, the RPAS EOI (AR-013), any specific ministerial meeting, or any procurement or policy decision. Separately, Buy NSW material identifies multiple Australian-based vendors capable of the relevant autonomous drone-in-a-box/BVLOS/remote-operations integration, including DJI-compatible systems - demonstrating that market alternatives and integration capability exist - but no evidence located establishes that any specific named example vendor supplied Moree, responded to the RPAS EOI, or has been selected by NSW Police.
determinations: DJI and DJI Technology Australia Pty Ltd each appear as client records of an active registered NSW lobbyist on the NSW Electoral Commission's lobbyist register, establishing a NSW lobbying footprint but not the specific dates or subject matter of any individual engagement.

No evidence located connects this lobbying footprint to the Moree trial, Michael Kemp, Yasmin Catley, the RPAS EOI, any specific ministerial meeting, or any procurement or policy decision - lobbying presence VERIFIED, influence over PolAir-Remote UNKNOWN/NOT ESTABLISHED, mirroring the source material's own classification.

Buy NSW material identifies multiple Australian-based vendors capable of the relevant drone-integration services, establishing that market alternatives exist; no evidence located establishes that any specific named example vendor supplied Moree, responded to the RPAS EOI, or has been selected by NSW Police.
mechanisms: A documented lobbying registration for a platform vendor can be read as implying influence over a specific procurement or policy outcome; the register itself does not establish that connection, and none has been located for PolAir-Remote specifically.
paths.boundary: No determination is made that DJI's NSW lobbying activity influenced, or was directed at, the Moree trial, the Kemp petition, or any NSW Police procurement or policy decision; only that a lobbying footprint is documented and no link to this case's subject matter has been located.

paths.title: Australian RPAS Incident History Establishes Non-Zero Failure Risk in the Broader Operating Environment; No Moree-Specific Incident Located
analysis: ATSB investigation AO-2021-001 documented a DJI Inspire 2 flyaway at Darling Harbour following compass failure/electromagnetic interference, resulting in loss of control and a collision, and separately characterised reported RPA flyaways as not a rare occurrence. ATSB is also currently investigating a May 2026 Sydney Harbour event in which 89 RPAS from a large drone swarm were lost following collisions with water/terrain. Both are drawn from Australia's own aviation-safety investigation record and establish RPAS failure as a documented, non-zero risk category in the Australian operating environment.

Neither documented incident involves the Dock 3/Matrice 4-series platform, NSW Police, or Moree, and the systems and contexts differ materially from Moree PolAir-Remote. No Moree or NSW Police Dock 3 crash or equivalent incident has been located in the public record; the finding establishes background failure risk in the broader operating environment, not any platform- or program-specific safety record.
determinations: ATSB investigation AO-2021-001 documented a DJI Inspire 2 flyaway at Darling Harbour (compass failure/electromagnetic interference, loss of control, collision) and separately characterised reported RPA flyaways as not rare, establishing RPAS failure as a documented risk category in the Australian aviation-safety record.

ATSB is separately investigating a May 2026 Sydney Harbour event in which 89 RPAS from a large drone swarm were lost following collisions with water/terrain - a second, more recent, documented Australian large-scale RPAS failure event.
Neither documented incident involves the Dock 3/Matrice 4-series platform, NSW Police, or Moree, and no Moree/NSW Police Dock 3 crash or equivalent incident has been located in the public record.
mechanisms: Incident history from a different RPAS product or operating context can be read as directly predictive of a distinct platform's own failure risk; establishing that RPAS flyaways are 'not rare' in the Australian record generally does not, by itself, establish anything about the Dock 3/Matrice 4-series platform's own reliability.
paths.boundary: No determination is made about the Dock 3/Matrice 4-series platform's own reliability, about any elevated or reduced failure risk specific to NSW Police's Moree deployment, or about whether an equivalent incident has occurred but gone unreported; the finding is limited to what Australia's own aviation-safety investigation record establishes about RPAS failure risk generally, and to the absence of a located Moree-specific incident.

paths.title: Existing Capability Baseline Requires an Incremental-Capability Justification, Not a Zero-Surveillance Comparison
analysis: Reading preserved/snapshot-10-2026-08-16.txt (F-185, F-186) against this case's existing cost- and network-architecture paths shows a distinct, previously-untouched question: whether the case for PolAir-Remote accounts for the surveillance and detection capability Kempsey already has. Kempsey Shire Council has reported operating more than 100 CCTV cameras, providing footage to NSW Police several times per month, with permanent coverage of multiple public locations. AR-073 uses this same existing-CCTV/MANPR fact only as one input to a regional network-node design question (how many docks, where); it does not address whether PolAir-Remote's own justification identifies what capability that existing baseline does not already provide. AR-005/AR-033/AR-071 address a materially different question - whether the program's cost claim and comparative economics are quantified - not whether the technology adds capability beyond what already exists.

NSW Police already operates conventional PolAir helicopters/fixed-wing aircraft with FLIR, high-definition video and live downlink, and holds a current seven-year Mobile Automatic Number Plate Recognition contract, alongside Kempsey Council's fixed CCTV network and existing ground patrol capacity. Because these assets address different operational problems (fixed-point coverage, vehicle detection, wide-area aerial observation, physical intervention), a methodologically sound assessment would test combinations of this existing capability against a 'drone or no drone' framing, rather than treat that binary framing as sufficient on its own.
determinations: Kempsey Shire Council operates more than 100 CCTV cameras and provides footage to NSW Police several times per month, with permanent coverage of multiple public locations, meaning a PolAir-Remote capability case would need to identify the specific incremental capability deficit left by that existing baseline (for example mobile tracking, thermal/night search, coverage beyond fixed camera fields, rapid incident assessment, or missing-person search), rather than compare the technology against an absence of surveillance capability.

NSW Police already operates conventional PolAir aircraft with FLIR/live downlink and a current seven-year Mobile Automatic Number Plate Recognition contract, alongside Kempsey's CCTV network and ground patrol capacity; because these assets address different operational problems, a methodologically valid comparison would test combinations of existing capability against a 'drone or no drone' framing, not that framing in isolation.

No public document located identifies the specific incremental capability deficit PolAir-Remote is intended to fill beyond Kempsey's existing fixed-camera, MANPR and conventional-PolAir baseline, or evaluates the technology against a bundled-alternative comparison rather than a binary one.
paths.boundary: No determination is made about whether PolAir-Remote does or does not add meaningful capability beyond Kempsey's existing surveillance/detection baseline, or about the outcome of any bundled-alternative comparison; only that a comparison against a zero-surveillance baseline is not the methodologically correct framing given the capability that already exists, and that no public source supplies the incremental-deficit or bundled comparison this would require.

paths.title: DJI Ecosystem Interoperability Creates a Structural Switching-Cost Path; No Public Ongoing Lifecycle/Migration Governance Located
analysis: Reading preserved/snapshot-10-2026-08-16.txt (F-187, F-188) against AR-050 (undisclosed future RPAS-panel contract terms, including exit rights and data-return obligations) and AR-056 (undisclosed decommissioning-mechanics plan for a program termination) shows a distinct, previously-untouched layer: technical vendor interoperability and the governance of an ongoing, operating platform's own lifecycle, neither of which either existing path reaches. DJI FlightHub 2 is documented as supporting DJI docks/aircraft only - it does not connect drones from other manufacturers, though it can integrate some third-party algorithms - and Dock 3 itself supports only the Matrice 4D series. The source material is explicit that NSW Police's actual backend architecture is not established and that existing vendor lock-in is accordingly not asserted; the finding is limited to the structural switching-cost path this documented interoperability limit creates if the stack is adopted deeply for workflows, data, training and automation.

Separately, FlightHub 2 is available as public-cloud or on-premises infrastructure, and DJI continues firmware/software updates and ecosystem changes over time. This creates an ongoing lifecycle-governance question distinct from AR-056's termination-mechanics question: what policy governs firmware support, battery/aircraft replacement, software support, data export/archival formats, credential revocation, and replacement-vendor migration while the program continues operating, not only if or when it ends. No public PolAir-Remote-specific lifecycle or migration plan addressing any of these has been located, and none of AR-013's, AR-050's or AR-056's own text addresses this ongoing-operation layer even in outline.
determinations: DJI FlightHub 2 is documented as supporting only DJI docks/aircraft (not other manufacturers' drones, though it can integrate some third-party algorithms), and Dock 3 supports only the Matrice 4D series, creating a documented technical interoperability limit that would carry non-trivial migration costs if the stack is adopted deeply for workflows, data, training and automation; NSW Police's actual backend architecture is not publicly established, so existing lock-in is not asserted, only the structural switching-cost path this interoperability limit creates.

No public PolAir-Remote-specific policy has been located addressing firmware support, battery/aircraft replacement, software support, data export/archival formats, credential revocation, or replacement-vendor migration - the ongoing lifecycle-governance questions that arise while a DJI-centred stack continues operating, distinct from AR-056's finding about decommissioning mechanics if the program is terminated.

This ongoing-lifecycle/migration-governance gap is distinct from, and unaddressed by, both AR-050's finding that eighteen terms of a possible future RPAS-panel contract are undisclosed and AR-056's finding that no decommissioning/termination-mechanics plan is public; no source located addresses vendor-migration or lifecycle governance for the current architecture while it continues operating.
mechanisms: Deep integration with a single-vendor ecosystem (DJI FlightHub 2, documented as exclusive to DJI docks/aircraft) can make future migration to another vendor progressively more costly the longer a lifecycle/migration governance policy remains unpublished; NSW Police's actual backend architecture is not established, so this describes a structural risk path, not an asserted present lock-in.
paths.boundary: No determination is made that vendor lock-in currently exists, that NSW Police's actual backend architecture creates the switching costs described, or that any migration or decommissioning has been attempted or refused; only that the platform's own documented interoperability limits create a structural switching-cost path, and that no public policy addresses ongoing lifecycle/migration governance at any layer checked.

paths.title: International Governance-Benchmark Comparators Show Stronger Transparency, Audit and Approval Gates Are Administratively Achievable Elsewhere
analysis: Reading preserved/snapshot-10-2026-08-16.txt (F-190 through F-193) against this case's own disclosure-gap findings (AR-016/AR-042/AR-043 on discoverability and escalation routes, AR-045 on retention/access/secondary-use, AR-047 on biometric/AI governance mechanics, and AR-054/AR-055 on decision-gate architecture) shows a distinct, previously-untouched category: none of this case's existing paths cites a comparator from another jurisdiction. The source material is explicit throughout that each comparator below is foreign and not binding on NSW; the finding is limited to what each demonstrates about administrative feasibility, not to any claim that NSW law requires an equivalent or that PolAir-Remote lacks one.

Chula Vista Police Department (California) publicly provides drone-activity dashboards and flight-history maps, states every flight is tracked for transparency, and its policy prohibits general surveillance/general patrol and unwarranted recording of places carrying a reasonable expectation of privacy. Litigation over Chula Vista's own drone records separately shows that a categorical refusal to release requested footage was rejected by a California appellate court, which recognised the footage still carries substantial privacy/redaction burdens - demonstrating that a mature, high-volume police drone program can generate a real records-access and redaction workload as an operational consequence of its own success, not merely a hypothetical risk.

The Baltimore persistent-aerial-surveillance litigation record documented that actual data retention did not initially match the program's own stated 45-day retention rule, showing that a written retention policy does not by itself establish that retention practice complies with it. New Zealand Police's two-stage technology-governance policy (applying before new technology adoption and before significant added functionality), UK ICO guidance requiring a Data Protection Impact Assessment before high-risk surveillance technology purchase/use, and US DOJ policy confining UAS use to authorised activities with annual privacy reviews are each documented as administratively operating models in their own jurisdictions.
determinations: Chula Vista Police Department (California) publicly provides drone-activity dashboards and flight-history maps, states every flight is tracked for transparency, and its policy prohibits general surveillance/general patrol and unwarranted recording of areas carrying a reasonable expectation of privacy - a foreign comparator demonstrating this class of transparency measure is administratively achievable for a police drone-in-a-box program, not a finding that NSW law requires it or that PolAir-Remote publishes an equivalent.

Litigation over Chula Vista's own drone records shows a categorical refusal to release requested footage was rejected by a California appellate court, which recognised the footage still carries substantial privacy/redaction burdens; this demonstrates that a mature, high-volume police drone program can generate a real records-access and redaction workload as an operational consequence, not that any equivalent case, obligation or workload exists for PolAir-Remote.

The Baltimore persistent-aerial-surveillance litigation record documented that actual data retention did not initially match the program's own stated 45-day rule, showing that a written retention policy does not by itself establish that retention practice complies with it; distinct from AR-045's finding that no PolAir-Remote-specific retention period is even disclosed, this shows that disclosure of a retention rule, if it occurred, would not alone establish implementation compliance without a separate audit mechanism, which is itself not shown to exist for PolAir-Remote.

New Zealand Police's two-stage technology-governance policy, UK ICO guidance requiring a Data Protection Impact Assessment before high-risk surveillance technology purchase/use, and US DOJ policy confining UAS use to authorised activities with annual privacy reviews are documented foreign comparators demonstrating that explicit pre-adoption and periodic technology-governance gates of the kind AR-047/AR-054 find undisclosed for PolAir-Remote are administratively achievable models elsewhere, not that NSW law requires their equivalent.
paths.boundary: No determination is made that NSW law requires, or that PolAir-Remote lacks, any of these specific governance mechanisms, that any of these foreign programs is otherwise comparable to PolAir-Remote in scale or legal context, or that adopting an equivalent would resolve any gap this case has identified; these are documented administrative comparators establishing feasibility elsewhere, not a finding of applicable NSW obligation or of any deficiency against a standard PolAir-Remote is bound by.

paths.title: Operational Tasking, Launch-Authority and Proactive-Patrol Threshold: NSW Police's Own Parliamentary Answer Confirms a Governing Policy Exists, Not Publicly Disclosed
analysis: The AE Primary Record Acquisition Register's Q705-Q709 (Section AE, EV-0793 through EV-0797) test whether the specific operational instruments governing day-to-day PolAir-Remote tasking are public - a narrower, more concrete layer than AR-010's reactive/proactive framing contradiction, AR-038's mission-data-schema gap, AR-042's private-property observation-boundary gap, or AR-054/AR-055's continuation-and-expansion decision-authority gap. NSW Police told Parliament that RPAS operations must comply with relevant NSWPF policies and procedures - an affirmative statement that a controlling operational policy exists - yet the current public NSW Police policy index does not expose any such controlling RPAS/PolAir-Remote-specific policy (Q705/EV-0793). No operator Standard Operating Procedure has been located publicly, even in a releasable or redacted form (Q706/EV-0794). Central management of RPAS operations by Aviation Command is independently verified elsewhere in this case's evidence base, but the exact rule or delegation establishing who holds launch and tasking authority for a specific mission is not public (Q707/EV-0795). And while public reporting independently verifies that proactive flying was contemplated for the Moree trial, no binding policy or threshold defining when proactive, as opposed to reactive or incident-responsive, patrol is authorised has been located (Q708/EV-0796).

This differs from AR-010's finding in kind, not only in specificity: AR-010 establishes that two public descriptions of the program's operating mode conflict and are unreconciled; this path establishes that NSW Police has itself affirmed, in a formal parliamentary answer, that a governing operational policy exists and applies - closing off any reading that no such instrument exists at all - while the instrument itself remains outside the public policy index NSW Police otherwise maintains. Q709/EV-0797 (mission-classification definitions) restates AR-038.1's already-established flight-type-classification finding almost exactly and is left unanchored here rather than duplicated, consistent with the discipline DEC-0009/DEC-0010 established. This path strengthens rather than duplicates YIELD-REQ-003, which already requests the operational policy and releasable SOPs governing launch authority, proactive-patrol rules, mission classification, recording and retention: it supplies the specific parliamentary-answer basis establishing that the requested policy is affirmatively confirmed to exist by NSW Police's own statement, not merely hoped to exist.
determinations: NSW Police told Parliament that RPAS operations must comply with relevant NSWPF policies and procedures, but the current public NSW Police policy index does not expose any controlling RPAS/PolAir-Remote-specific policy - the governing instrument's existence is affirmed, its content is not public.

No PolAir-Remote operator Standard Operating Procedure, and no rule establishing who holds launch/tasking authority for a specific mission despite Aviation Command's verified central management role, has been publicly located.

No binding policy or threshold defining when proactive, as opposed to reactive, patrol is authorised has been publicly located, despite public reporting independently verifying that proactive flying was contemplated for the Moree trial.
mechanisms: A parliamentary assurance that operations 'comply with relevant policies' functions as institutional reassurance without the underlying policy itself being disclosed, the same pattern AR-010 and AR-022 identify in other public statements about this program.
paths.boundary: No determination is made about the content of NSW Police's internal operational policy, SOPs, launch-authority delegation, or proactive-patrol threshold, or that any specific mission was launched or flown proactively without proper internal authorisation; only that NSW Police's own parliamentary answer confirms a governing policy exists while none of these specific instruments is publicly disclosed.

paths.title: Detection Cannot Substitute for Downstream Response Capacity, and This Expansion's Workforce-Allocation Justification Is Undisclosed
analysis: Deep Research Snapshot 5 (F-056, EV-0095) documents a concrete substitution limit distinct in kind from AR-037's structural detection/response-capacity-scaling mechanism: existing Mid North Coast specialist domestic-violence staffing is documented as thin across a large district, and a drone that helps locate an alleged offender does not itself perform victim liaison, risk assessment, AVO management, evidence preparation or follow-up - functions a detection technology cannot substitute for regardless of how far or how fast its own detection capacity is expanded. AR-037 already establishes that no public evidence shows local frontline staffing was increased alongside PolAir-Remote's own aerial-observation capability; this path identifies a specific, named function class - domestic-violence response - that a docked aerial asset structurally cannot replace, distinct from AR-037's more general capacity-imbalance mechanism.

Separately, Snapshot 5 (F-057, EV-0096) records the NSW Audit Office's own general finding that NSW Police lacks a comprehensive workload-based staffing and resource-allocation model, and that political commitments can influence staffing placement without an analysis of actual workload. This is a general finding about NSW Police resourcing decisions, not one directed at PolAir-Remote. AR-002 already establishes that Kempsey's own PolAir-Remote expansion was publicly contemplated by government before the Kemp petition amplified it - a government-contemplated-then-petition-amplified origin, not a workload-analysis-driven one. Read together, no public record establishes that this specific expansion decision was itself grounded in a workload-based capability-deficit analysis, as distinct from the political/constituency-demand pathway AR-002 already documents for how this expansion became publicly visible.
determinations: A drone that helps locate an alleged offender in a domestic-violence incident does not itself perform victim liaison, risk assessment, AVO management, evidence preparation or follow-up; existing Mid North Coast specialist domestic-violence staffing capacity is documented as thin across a large district, independent of any change in aerial-detection capacity.

The NSW Audit Office has found generally that NSW Police lacks a comprehensive workload-based staffing/resource allocation model, and that political commitments can influence staffing placement without an analysis of actual workload; no public record establishes that this specific PolAir-Remote expansion decision was grounded in a workload-based capability-deficit analysis, as distinct from the government-contemplated-then-petition-amplified pathway AR-002 already documents for it.
paths.boundary: No determination is made that domestic-violence response outcomes have actually been affected by PolAir-Remote's deployment, that this specific expansion decision was made internally without any workload analysis, or that the Audit Office's general finding was directed at PolAir-Remote specifically; only that (a) a documented capability gap exists between what aerial detection performs and what domestic-violence response requires, and (b) a documented general pattern of non-workload-based NSW Police resourcing decisions has not been shown, for this expansion, not to apply.

paths.title: Arrests and Charges Are Not NSW Police's Own Recorded Measure, and Detection-Driven Ascertainment Bias Further Undermines Any Before/After Comparison
analysis: Snapshot 5 (F-082, EV-0121) records that NSW Police's own parliamentary evidence states arrests are not a category its systems record: when asked for arrest counts, it substituted "unique legal actions" with an explicit caution that a legal action can link to multiple incidents and offence categories. This is a different and more specific gap than AR-004's reproducibility finding (that the petition's aggregate totals have not been reproduced from a published dataset) and AR-024.4's deterrence-metric limitation (that arrest volume cannot serve as a deterrence-success measure): here, the term the petition uses - "arrests" - does not correspond to any category NSW Police itself uses to record its own activity. F-083 (EV-0122) extends the same definitional mismatch to any charge or offence total, which does not map one-to-one onto separate criminal episodes or unique offenders.

Separately, F-086 and F-087 (EV-0125, EV-0126) record ascertainment bias - the documented general finding that increased police/service contact and detection can raise recorded activity independent of any change in underlying conduct - as an established measurement risk that applies specifically to a detection technology like PolAir-Remote: because the platform is designed to increase detection probability, a raw before/after activity-count comparison cannot separate a genuine change in underlying offending from a change in the probability that existing offending is detected and recorded. This is a distinct mechanism from AR-006's multi-program confounding, which concerns apportioning effect between concurrent interventions rather than the measurement mechanism itself; F-088 (EV-0127) applies this same before/after limitation specifically to Moree's co-occurring Soteria targeting, bail enforcement, diversion and PolAir-Remote activity.

F-074 and F-084/F-085 (EV-0113, EV-0123, EV-0124) record that Operation Soteria's own stated design - combining overt operational response with early identification and diversion - and the NSW regional youth-crime response's own stated objective of breaking reoffending cycles and preventing at-risk youth entering the justice system, together establish that arrest/charge volume was never the stated primary success measure for the broader enforcement architecture PolAir-Remote operates within. This reinforces, from the stated-objectives side, the counting-methodology problem identified above; it does not itself propose what PolAir-Remote's evaluation measure should be, only records what the enforcement architecture's own already-stated objectives are.
determinations: NSW Police's own parliamentary evidence states that arrests are not a category its systems record; when asked for arrest counts it substituted "unique legal actions", with an explicit caution that a legal action can link to multiple incidents and offence categories - meaning the petition's "100+ arrests" figure does not correspond to any category NSW Police itself uses to measure its own activity, a distinct gap from AR-004's reproducibility finding and AR-024.4's deterrence-metric limitation.

The same definitional mismatch extends to any charge or offence total: charges and offences in operational reporting do not map one-to-one onto separate criminal episodes or unique offenders, so an activity count cannot be read as a person-level or incident-level outcome measure.

Ascertainment bias - a documented general finding that increased detection can raise recorded activity independent of any change in underlying conduct - is an established measurement risk for detection technologies and applies specifically to PolAir-Remote: a raw before/after activity-count comparison, including of Moree's own co-occurring Soteria and bail-enforcement activity, cannot separate genuine offending change from detection-probability change, a distinct mechanism from AR-006's already-established multi-program confounding.

Operation Soteria's own stated two-pillar design (enforcement and diversion) and the NSW regional youth-crime response's own stated objective of breaking reoffending cycles establish that arrest/charge volume was never the stated primary success measure for the enforcement architecture PolAir-Remote operates within, reinforcing AR-081.1-AR-081.3's counting-methodology finding from the stated-objectives side.
paths.boundary: No determination is made that the petition's specific figures are inflated, fabricated, or that ascertainment bias has actually occurred at Moree in any particular direction or magnitude; only that (a) the terms the petition uses do not match categories NSW Police's own evidence says it records, and (b) any before/after activity-count comparison of a detection technology carries an inherent, undemonstrated-as-controlled-for ascertainment-bias confound distinct from AR-006's already-established multi-program confounding.

paths.title: The Petition's Own Text Leaves Both Its Geographic Scope and Any Safeguard Conditions Undefined
analysis: Kemp's Oxley electorate covers 9,325.32 square kilometres and includes Kempsey, Bellingen, Nambucca Heads, Wauchope and many other inland and coastal communities. The petition calls for expansion to "the Mid North Coast" without defining whether that means a single Kempsey node, Oxley-electorate-wide coverage, Mid North Coast Police District coverage, or a distributed regional network - so the specific rollout footprint the petition asks for is not itself settled by its own wording. YIELD-REQ-006 already seeks the coverage and feasibility design that would resolve this at the institutional-planning level; this path establishes that the ambiguity exists at the level of the petition's own text as well, not only in NSW Police's undisclosed planning.

Separately, the petition's own wording asks for expansion and prioritisation of regional communities without stating any condition on proactive-patrol scope, recording or retention practice, AI or biometric use, Aboriginal-impact reporting, flight transparency, independent evaluation, or a stop/go threshold. This is a different question from AR-010's and AR-011's operating-mode contradictions, which concern conflicting public statements about how the existing Moree deployment already operates; this path concerns what the petition itself does and does not ask for, independent of anything NSW Police has said.
determinations: The petition's call to expand to "the Mid North Coast" does not define whether that means a Kempsey node, Oxley-electorate-wide coverage, Mid North Coast Police District coverage, or a distributed regional network, despite the electorate spanning 9,325.32 square kilometres across multiple distinct communities.

The petition's own wording does not state any condition on proactive-patrol scope, recording/retention practice, AI or biometric use, Aboriginal-impact reporting, flight transparency, independent evaluation, or a stop/go threshold for the expansion it requests.
paths.boundary: No determination is made that the petition ought to have specified a rollout footprint or safeguard conditions, or that its signatories intended something different from what its text says; this path records only what the petition's own wording does and does not state, not what it should have stated.

paths.title: No Documented Record Establishes When Kemp Was Briefed on PolAir-Remote, or That a PolAir-Remote-Specific Written Question From Him Exists
analysis: No public record locates when Michael Kemp was first briefed on PolAir-Remote, who briefed him, what material was supplied, or whether the formal Moree evaluation was provided to him. This is a specific documentary gap distinct from AR-002's broader finding that the petition sits inside a pre-existing institutional trajectory that predates it: AR-002 establishes that the trajectory itself (statewide procurement, the Aviation Command operating-model review, the Police Minister's own naming of Kempsey) existed independently of Kemp; this path establishes that Kemp's own specific point of entry into that trajectory is undocumented on the public record checked.

Kemp's parliamentary record includes extensive policing and regional-crime questions, and AR-002.3 already establishes his own prior transparency-scrutiny practice through Q&A 6484's KPI/public-reporting demand. Despite this record, a targeted search did not locate a written question from Kemp specifically demanding the Moree evaluation, trial costs, the petition's statistic sources, safeguards, or stop/go criteria. This absence does not establish that no such question exists, and no inference is drawn about why a PolAir-Remote-specific question has not been located; it is recorded only as a gap in the public record checked, to be read alongside AR-002.4's existing finding that no inference of impropriety is drawn from Kemp's use of the petition itself.
determinations: No public record establishes when, by whom, or with what material Kemp was first briefed on PolAir-Remote, or whether the formal Moree evaluation was supplied to him - a specific documentary gap distinct from AR-002's broader pre-existing-institutional-trajectory finding.

A targeted search of Kemp's parliamentary record did not locate a written question from him specifically on the Moree evaluation, trial costs, petition-statistic sourcing, safeguards, or stop/go criteria, despite his extensive general policing/regional-crime record and his own KPI/public-reporting demand already established at AR-002.3; this is not proof no such record exists.
paths.boundary: No determination is made about Kemp's motives, knowledge, or any undisclosed briefing that may in fact have occurred, and no inference is drawn that he sought to shield PolAir-Remote from the same scrutiny he has applied to other programs; only that the public record checked does not establish a briefing timeline or a PolAir-Remote-specific written question from him.

paths.title: Retention, Disclosure and Deletion of PolAir-Derived Material Are Governed by Several Distinct Legal Regimes, Not One Privacy Question
analysis: Beyond AR-019.2's already-established finding that CASA's seven-year aviation-record requirement means "not recorded" does not equal "no government record exists", the State Records Act 1998 (s 21) separately and independently restricts unauthorised abandonment, disposal, transfer, damage or alteration of any State record - so the same "no video does not mean no record" logic rests on two independent legal sources, not one.
